piano nobile.definition: In traditional hierarchical building design, the principal inhabited floor of a building, typically the main residence level accessible by initial flights of stairs.
piano nobile.context: The main level, where a house's owner resided, was called the piano nobile, and was accessible by two or three flights of stairs, while the cramped garrets, just below the roof, commonly housed servants.

enclosed room.definition: A room with a single designated entry point and walls that create psychological and physical separation from surrounding spaces, characteristic of Victorian architectural design.
enclosed room.context: Enter was via a single door on one wall, leaving other walls closed off from their surroundings. We might perceive such an enclosed room as a discrete entity, a place where awareness of the external spaces and events occurring beyond its walls is not necessarily present.

cast.definition: The informational content of hardness; a statement or claim about the future state of the world that is made hard by a system.
cast.context: First, what is the hardness about? What is the informational content of the hardness? I will call this the cast. The cast is the 'thing that is hard,' and it always takes the form of a statement or claim about the future.

atom hardness.definition: Hardness sourced from the physical properties of the universe, including matter, physical laws, and natural constants that make certain future states predictable.
atom hardness.context: Atom hardness refers to hardness that is sourced from the physical properties of our universe. This hardness includes not just literal atoms (i.e., matter, physical stuff), but all other properties of nature like physical laws and constants.

institution hardness.definition: Hardness created through organized human behavior, where groups of people act in predictable ways over time to enforce rules and make future states reliable.
institution hardness.context: In other cases, the source of hardness might be an institution. A contract is only hard if there is an institution that makes it so. Groups of people—lawyers, judges, police officers—who share a common understanding of how to work together.

blockchain hardness.definition: A natively digital source of hardness created through cryptography, networked software, and commoditized human incentives that make digital records and programs permanently reliable.
blockchain hardness.context: Recently, we've invented a new way to create hardness: blockchains. Using an elegant combination of cryptography, networked software, and commoditized human incentives, we are able to create software and digital records that have a degree of permanence.

institution.definition: A broad category of organized human groups including legal systems, governments, corporations, and religious bodies that act predictably to create hardness and enforce rules.
institution.context: Institution here is an extremely broad category, including: legal systems, legislatures, police forces, governments, central banks and other monetary authorities, private banks, corporations, startups, religious institutions.

credible neutrality.definition: A system characteristic where the protocol cannot be perceived as favoring any particular participant or faction, essential for maintaining consensus among diverse stakeholders.
credible neutrality.context: Isolated entities cannot fully enclose blockspace production systems without compromising crucial characteristics, i.e., availability, credible neutrality, censorship resistance.
credible neutrality.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

composability.definition: A technical and policy design principle where protocols, apps, and governance components can be combined, separated, and reconfigured independently while remaining functional.
composability.context: The key is that each app is composable and interoperable, meaning they are able to share users and data, and can be copied and run anywhere, by anyone. These features allow protocols to integrate seamlessly with each other when necessary.
composability.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

hyperstructures.definition: Protocols built on blockchain hardness that can theoretically run forever without requiring maintenance or central coordination because their foundations are permanently reliable.
hyperstructures.context: Ethereum enables hyperstructures—protocols that can run forever—because blockchains provide a native source of hardness that makes the structures built on top of them extremely likely to persist into the future.

trustless.definition: A system designed to function without requiring participants to trust any single entity or intermediary; trust is instead distributed across protocol rules and cryptographic verification.
trustless.context: Trustless protocols enable parties to transact and coordinate even when they do not trust each other or any intermediary.

decentralized finance (defi).definition: Financial systems built on blockchain hardness that recreate complex financial relationships without requiring institutional intermediaries.
decentralized finance (defi).context: Ethereum enables decentralized finance (defi) because it lets us create programmable hardness sufficient to recreate the complex intersecting web of relationships that characterize traditional finance.

web3.definition: An ecosystem of digital services, protocols, and applications whose infrastructure is grounded primarily in blockchain hardness rather than institutional hardness.
web3.context: Ethereum enables web3: an ecosystem of web services, protocols, applications, and communities whose foundations are built primarily on blockchain hardness rather than institutional hardness.

source of hardness.definition: The underlying mechanism or system that makes a cast (future claim) hard; atoms, institutions, or blockchains.
source of hardness.context: Second, there is the source of hardness. The source of hardness is the reason that the cast can be hard in the first place. It is what the cast is made out of: atoms, institutions, or blockchains.

programmable hardness.definition: The ability to customize and create arbitrary future claims that are made reliable through software running on blockchains.
programmable hardness.context: Just as institutions let us create hard casts with any arbitrary content that can be interpreted and executed by humans, Ethereum lets us create hard casts with arbitrary content that can be interpreted and executed by a computer.

cryptographic hardness.definition: Hardness derived from the mathematical properties of cryptographic systems that make it computationally infeasible to forge or alter digital information.
cryptographic hardness.context: The specific cryptographic tools used by blockchains are public and available for study, and generally their properties are very well understood. The cost of attacking the system to subvert it (e.g., through a so-called 51% attack) is known and we can estimate it accurately.

51% attack.definition: An attack on a blockchain where a malicious actor controls over half the network's computing power, allowing them to subvert the system's hardness.
51% attack.context: The cost of attacking the system to subvert it (e.g., through a so-called 51% attack) is known and we can estimate it accurately.

natively digital.definition: Systems or properties that are inherently designed for and dependent on digital technology and internet infrastructure.
natively digital.context: Blockchains are natively digital. They create hardness about software, data, and programs. Anyone with an internet connection can access and interact with a blockchain.

mainnet.definition: The main operational blockchain network where applications are deployed with high assurance of permanence.
mainnet.context: Applications that are deployed on mainnet will stay there, letting developers build on top of what has already been built, with high confidence that those foundations can never crumble beneath them.

atoms, institutions, and blockchains (ai.definition: The three sources of hardness available to human civilization for creating predictability and reliability in complex systems.
atoms, institutions, and blockchains (ai.context: Atoms, Institutions, and Blockchains are some of the raw materials this infrastructure is built with. Just as an architect must carefully plan not only the design of a building, but also the materials used to construct that design, so must we carefully consider the materials for our civilization's infrastructure.

unprotocolized knowledge.definition: Information, theories, and research that develop and circulate outside formal institutional knowledge production systems, particularly through internet communities and informal channels rather than through peer review and academic publication.
unprotocolized knowledge.context: There's something powerful about how online seed oil researchers have developed their hypotheses in an unprotocolized way. Seed oils are at the center of a variety of theories, identified as the culprit behind issues ranging from the obesity epidemic to chronic disease.

knowledge protocols.definition: Formal systems and processes (like peer review) that legitimate and validate knowledge claims, evolving to process information behaviors enabled by the internet and emerging internet-based knowledge production.
knowledge protocols.context: Knowledge protocols like peer review have evolved to enable vast amounts of information to be validated, but further development is required to process the information behaviors the internet has enabled.

populist paradigms.definition: Popular, contested theories and ideas that gain widespread traction outside academic institutions, often spreading through internet communities and challenging established scientific paradigms.
populist paradigms.context: These 'populist paradigms,' to twist Thomas Kuhn's term, present a dual challenge. On the one hand, they obviously have spread largely outside the university, bypassing and thus failing to meet the rigorous standards for adjudication that typically accompany scientific claims.

paradigm refugees.definition: Scientists and researchers who are systematically excluded from grants and publishing opportunities because their work challenges the dominant paradigm in their field, forcing them to abandon their original research.
paradigm refugees.context: The decades-long silent embargo forced some researchers to pivot to other topics, creating a class of 'paradigm refugees' unable to continue their original work in a hostile environment.

reasonable insufficiency.definition: The emergence of unmanaged maladaptive phenomena and systemic problems that arise as a consequence of protocols that have become too successful and created new challenges they cannot resolve.
reasonable insufficiency.context: Perhaps this quality of protocols might be called their reasonable insufficiency: The emergence of unmanaged maladaptive phenomena around too-successful protocols.

republic of letters.definition: A historical network of long-distance intellectual correspondence and exchange among 15th-16th century European scholars that preceded formal institutional knowledge production and inspired the development of academic journals.
republic of letters.context: As 15th-century scholars shared thoughts, news, and responses across national boundaries, they began to understand themselves as participating in a global scholarly conversation, the Republic of Letters.

epistemic tribalism.definition: A condition of knowledge production in which different groups or communities each adopt incompatible frameworks of truth and evidence, making consensus or shared understanding increasingly difficult.
epistemic tribalism.context: To members of the establishment, the internet's superspeed and superabundance of information creates a condition of 'epistemic tribalism' or 'post-truth.'

context collapse.definition: The phenomenon where the internet eliminates distinctions between academic and public spheres, causing information and communication designed for one audience to reach multiple, unintended audiences simultaneously.
context collapse.context: The alternative view is more realistic and more optimistic: the internet merely collapses the context between academia and the public, leading to new information behaviors that our knowledge production protocols aren't designed to handle.

feral scholars.definition: Unaffiliated amateur researchers and fact-checkers who investigate, verify, and circulate information independently, often in response to gaps or distrust in mainstream academic institutions.
feral scholars.context: Combine this with 'feral scholars' who fact-check, research, and circulate supposedly reputable information in response to the drama.

internet of beefs.definition: A social media ecosystem characterized by ongoing, highly publicized conflicts and disputes between public figures and their followers, often organized around ideological or lifestyle positions.
internet of beefs.context: In the chaotic space outside the jurisdiction of scholarly protocols, in the subscriber lists of influencers' Patreons, a horde of enthusiasts comes into play. Here is where the dynamics resemble less a scientific forum and more the 'Internet of Beefs.'

coercive citation.definition: The practice by journal editors of compelling authors to cite articles that benefit the journal's impact scores, representing a corruption of the peer review and citation system.
coercive citation.context: Journals, too, exhibit this overeffective quality, having extended far beyond their original function... their importance to the careers of young researchers has led to predatory practices, like charging exorbitant rates for publication and employing 'coercive citation': editors strong-arming authors to cite articles that benefit their journals' impact scores.

pre-paradigm theory.definition: An emerging set of hypotheses and approaches that have not yet achieved the status of a dominant, institutionally-validated scientific paradigm but may be collectively compelling enough to warrant serious investigation.
pre-paradigm theory.context: Nevertheless, these speculations may collectively be compelling enough to be considered a viable pre-paradigm theory. The causes of America's obesity and diabetes crises are questions that currently have no established paradigmatic answers.

dyoresearchers.definition: Amateur scientists and independent researchers who conduct their own investigations and experiments, typically drawing on freely available online knowledge and documentation.
dyoresearchers.context: The products of intellectual labor now live freely online, inspiring swaths of DYOResearchers.

citizen science.definition: Scientific research conducted by non-professional scientists, often amateurs or hobbyists, who contribute data collection, analysis, or experimentation under the framework of formal studies.
citizen science.context: Recent improvements in mobile sensors and smartphones have unlocked new opportunities for citizen science and crowdsourcing.

datafication.definition: The process of converting various aspects of human experience and activity into quantifiable data that can be recorded, analyzed, and used in research and decision-making.
datafication.context: The increasing datafication of health via biometrics points to future evolutions that may be possible for both scientific and internet health communities.

biomonitoring devices.definition: Wearable or portable technologies that measure and track biological indicators such as heart rate, sleep patterns, and other health metrics for personal health tracking or research purposes.
biomonitoring devices.context: Widely available biomonitoring devices could bring down the high cost of quantified selfhood.

participatory science.definition: Scientific research conducted with direct involvement and collaboration from non-professional community members in design, data collection, and evaluation of results.
participatory science.context: the internet making possible a 'global spasm of participatory science.'

epistemic uncertainty.definition: A state of doubt or lack of certainty about what can be known, believed, or validated as true within an information environment.
epistemic uncertainty.context: As it stands, we lack the organizing models necessary to deal with the epistemic uncertainty they create to validate their ideas.

quantified selfhood.definition: The practice of systematically measuring, tracking, and analyzing one's own biological metrics and health data using personal biometric devices and self-experimentation.
quantified selfhood.context: Widely available biomonitoring devices could bring down the high cost of quantified selfhood.

workplace productivity protocols.definition: Intentional patterns of human behavior designed to increase an organization's capability to outperform itself, prescribing a choreography for objects, bodies, and brains across meetings and communications.
workplace productivity protocols.context: Borrowing from this framing, workplace productivity protocols can be defined as intentional patterns of human behavior that increase the capability of an organization to outperform itself. These protocols prescribe a choreography for objects and bodies and brains and brains, a dance notation spanning months of run time on the stage of meeting rooms and emails.
workplace productivity protocols.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol dysphoria.definition: A state of dissatisfaction or distress experienced by workers when inhabiting ossified or misaligned productivity protocols that no longer serve their actual work needs.
protocol dysphoria.context: A protocolized framing of a bullshit job would be any worker experiencing what Summer of Protocols researcher Angela Walch calls protocol dysphoria.
protocol dysphoria.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol identity.definition: The particular role and set of responsibilities a worker assumes when entering a workplace as part of the larger system of protocols that govern organizational behavior.
protocol identity.context: These organizations are in effect systems of protocols that a worker inhabits when entering a workplace, taking on a particular protocol identity depending on their role.
protocol identity.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol evolution.definition: A theoretical framework explaining how safety and functionality in protocols gradually improve over time as humans learn from experience, invent new solutions, and adapt existing systems to changing conditions.
protocol evolution.context: Tracing the history of safety protocols in coal mining over two centuries, he develops a general theory of protocol evolution that attempts to explain how safety gradually improves as humans learn, invent, and adapt.
protocol evolution.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

exit to protocol.definition: A form of organizational retirement in which an organization ceases operations while publicly sharing its workplace protocols and operational knowledge, allowing new communities and organizations to inherit and evolve these patterns.
exit to protocol.context: Instead, through retiring and sharing some of its workplace protocols publically, this exit may shape many and new communities. This we might call an exit to protocol.
exit to protocol.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

whale fall.definition: An ecological process where a dead whale sinks to the ocean floor and its decomposition creates a nutrient-rich habitat that enables the rapid evolution of new species adapted to those conditions.
whale fall.context: An exit to protocol could be compared to a whale fall in ocean ecosystems, where the death of a whale and its subsequent decay process after falling to the ocean floor creates an energy-rich habitat and frees up nutrients to incubate rapidly evolving new life forms.
whale fall.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

adaptive radiation.definition: The ecological process by which new species rapidly evolve and diversify in response to the novel environmental conditions created by a whale fall or similar nutrient-rich habitat.
adaptive radiation.context: New species are commonly created through this process, known as adaptive radiation.
adaptive radiation.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

exit to community.definition: A movement that helps startups mature into community ownership by their stakeholders rather than pursuing acquisition or public stock offerings.
exit to community.context: Misaligned-incentive bullshit jobs might find a solution in the movement of Exit to Community, a movement that helps startups 'aim to mature into ownership by their community of stakeholders' rather than 'aiming for an acquisition by a more established company or a public stock offering.'
exit to community.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

role in a box.definition: A protocol system design that conveys the people and their relationships to data, spaces, and other people by encapsulating a role with preset levels of access, permissions, and incentives within an organization.
role in a box.context: The protocol system conveys the people and their relationship to data, spaces, and other people, describing it as a 'role in a box' with different preset levels of access, permissions, and incentives to represent and augment the organization.
role in a box.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

hats protocol.definition: A digital protocol that empowers groups to delegate responsibilities to contributors while giving them necessary authorities and installing accountability mechanisms to ensure task completion in distributed work environments.
hats protocol.context: Hats empowers groups to get things done by delegating responsibilities to the right contributors, giving them the hard and soft authorities they need to do their work, and installing real-time accountability mechanisms to ensure people follow through.
hats protocol.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

bullshit jobs.definition: Forms of employment that are so completely pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even employees cannot justify their existence, though they feel obliged to pretend otherwise.
bullshit jobs.context: Rather than experiencing protocol death through abandonment, the agile industrial complex creates an entire workforce engaged in what David Graeber called bullshit jobs—a group of workers kept employed under imbalanced power structures that encourage keeping up the pretenses of unnecessary work.
bullshit jobs.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

intellectual monopoly capitalism.definition: An economic system where corporations prioritize the capture and management of intellectual assets and knowledge as their most strategic resources, with learning itself becoming the primary corporate goal.
intellectual monopoly capitalism.context: The rise of intellectual monopoly capitalism presents a new buyer of workplace protocols for the sake of the protocols themselves, and not necessarily for their resulting productivity.
intellectual monopoly capitalism.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

bannister effect.definition: A phenomenon where organizational or emergent groups feel more confident about adopting new methods after seeing that success was possible with them, inspired by a celebratory rather than crisis-driven retirement.
bannister effect.context: Retirement that ends on a celebratory note allows for the Bannister Effect, where organizations or emergent groups may feel more confident about adopting the new methods through seeing that it was possible to achieve success with them.
bannister effect.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

metawork.definition: The documentation and operational processes of how work is performed, distinct from the actual work product itself; the practices and systems that enable and organize the primary work.
metawork.context: Such generous documentation and sharing of the metawork of a studio or any place of knowledge work is beyond rare in an industry where most documents are labeled confidential and nondisclosure agreements are signed.
metawork.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

selection pressures.definition: Institutional, structural, or incentive-based forces that constrain how protocols can evolve and adapt, often preventing necessary mutations that would improve protocol fitness.
selection pressures.context: However, the power dynamics in a workplace can impose selection pressures that prevent protocols from adapting through mutation, resulting in productivity protocols that become unfit for purpose.
selection pressures.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol death.definition: The process of a protocol-based world or system ending, understood as a decision-making process with duration rather than an instantaneous event, with implications for preservation and memorialization.
protocol death.context: The essay is accompanied by a taxonomy of possible protocol-deaths and a series of proposals for how to kill worlds.

dumb storage.definition: A practice of archiving organizational knowledge and resources in sealed or inaccessible formats that prevent their use or evolution by others, keeping them dormant for potential future recreation.
dumb storage.context: An organization might have kept confidential to maximize future consulting fees, or as Friend puts it in Good Death, sealed in 'dumb storage' so that the 'fantasy of recreating the thing being archived potentially exists.'
dumb storage.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

agile industrial complex.definition: A self-perpetuating ecosystem of consultants, thought leaders, and institutions that profit from continuous promotion and implementation of agile methodologies, creating perverse incentives that prevent protocol evolution.
agile industrial complex.context: This stuckness has characteristics comparable to the ossification of internet protocols. Agile development expert Daniel Mezick's 2016 essay, The Agile Industrial Complex, presents a fantastic case study of how a productivity protocol system has stagnated.
agile industrial complex.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

misaligned incentives.definition: Organizational structures or reward systems where individual workers' incentives diverge from the overall organization's actual productivity needs, contributing to the creation of unnecessary work.
misaligned incentives.context: Flunkies, duct tapers, and type 2 taskmasters exist as a result of misaligned incentives and unbalanced power structures.
misaligned incentives.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

safety protocols.definition: Intentional patterns of constraint on human behavior designed to reduce injury, disease, and death in work environments.
safety protocols.context: I define these as intentional patterns of constraint on human behavior that reduce injury, disease, and death. Safety protocols have evolved in lockstep with changes in the industrial environment.

dynamic non-event.definition: A sustained absence of accidents or negative outcomes resulting from successful human actions and moment-to-moment adjustments, which our brains fail to notice because they lack the discrete, eventful quality of accidents.
dynamic non-event.context: Safety is a dynamic non-event. Talking about safety (and health) is difficult because it is a sustained absence of events, not an event itself.

limit of unacceptable performance.definition: A threshold below which action outcomes become noticeable to human attention and trigger awareness or concern, distinguishing successful from failed performances.
limit of unacceptable performance.context: After a while, the only actions that catch our attention are those with outcome values below the 'limit of unacceptable performance'.

protocol-based social order.definition: A social arrangement with new norms, divisions of labor, and decision-making hierarchies that emerge to enforce and sustain behavioral constraints established by protocols.
protocol-based social order.context: New norms, divisions of labor, and decision-making hierarchies emerge to enforce such constraints. This results in a new protocol-based social order.

chokedamp.definition: Carbonic acid gas (CO2) found in coal mines that acts as an asphyxiant, historically identified as a hazard when a candle flame dimmed or extinguished near floor level.
chokedamp.context: chokedamp: stythe, damp, or blackdamp; carbonic acid gas; an asphyxiant gas. Chokedamp is heavier than air; miners would hold a candle near the floor. If it dimmed or went out, it was time to go.

firedamp.definition: Methane gas (carburetted hydrogen) found in coal mines that is highly explosive, historically addressed by miners preemptively igniting gas buildups.
firedamp.context: firedamp: methane gas/carburetted hydrogen; a highly explosive gas. Miners avoided firedamp by preemptively igniting buildups.

afterdamp.definition: A mixture of carbon monoxide, firedamp, and nitrogen produced after mine explosions that acts as both an asphyxiant and poisonous gas.
afterdamp.context: afterdamp: mix of carbon monoxide, firedamp, and nitrogen; an asphyxiant and poisonous gas.

stinkdamp.definition: Hydrogen sulfide gas found in coal mines, a poisonous gas historically identified by its distinctive odor.
stinkdamp.context: stinkdamp: hydrogen sulfide; a poisonous gas.

bell pit.definition: An early method of coal extraction from the 13th century using a narrow vertical shaft with a widened bottom chamber, abandoned once structural instability appeared and a new shaft was sunk nearby.
bell pit.context: As early as the 13th century, Europeans started to mine coal in bell pits. Miners sunk bell pits to about 30 feet below ground, with a narrow mouth, and dug wider at the bottom.

drift mine.definition: An early coal mining method in which miners dug a near-horizontal slope into a hillside or cliff rather than sinking a vertical shaft, used in terrain where vertical shafts were impractical.
drift mine.context: Drift mines were another early method of coal extraction. Miners dug a near-horizontal slope into a hillside or cliff, rather than digging a vertical shaft in a field.

piece wage.definition: A compensation system in which workers are paid based on the amount of work output (e.g., coal produced) rather than time spent working, creating economic incentives to prioritize productivity over safety.
piece wage.context: miners were often paid a piece wage (by the amount of coal produced, rather than time spent mining). Lack of supervision plus the incentive of piece wages led miners to trade safety for productivity.

the carbon flywheel.definition: The period (1700-1850 A.D.) when the introduction of steam engines and industrial machinery created a self-reinforcing cycle of increased coal demand and production expansion.
the carbon flywheel.context: After centuries of incremental progress, the coal industry had a big bang. With the industrial revolution came steam engines, boilers, coal furnaces, new machinery, and cheaper steel. These technologies enabled a new flywheel of productivity in the coal industry.

root cause analysis.definition: An investigative method used after industrial accidents to identify the underlying cause of failures, initially assumed to be human error before researchers shifted focus to systemic and organizational factors.
root cause analysis.context: First, root cause analysis led safety experts to assume incidents were being caused by human error. If the technology is safe, then it must be the humans who mess up.

safety culture.definition: The collective values, attitudes, and practices within an organization that prioritize and reinforce safe behavior, as distinct from technical engineering approaches to safety.
safety culture.context: The focus turned to sociology instead of psychology. Protocols to improve 'safety culture' came about. Take Five (taking a few minutes to consider the risks and safety measures required for a task), Safety Walk (management walking through a workplace to identify and address hazards), Poka-Yoke...

systems theory (in accident prevention).definition: An approach holding that accidents result from unexpected interactions between tightly coupled components within complex systems and are therefore inherently unpredictable and 'normal' despite prevention efforts.
systems theory (in accident prevention).context: Finally, systems theory came along—holding that 'unexpected interactions' between 'tightly coupled' components within a system cause accidents, and that such accidents are unpredictable. Ultimately, experts found that accidents are 'normal.'

normal accidents.definition: The concept that accidents are inherent and inevitable consequences of complex, tightly coupled systems despite rigorous safety measures, as both preventable and unprevantable phenomena coexist.
normal accidents.context: These two statements are both true: all accidents are preventable and we cannot prevent all accidents.

health protocols.definition: Behavioral constraints designed to prevent cumulative, irreparable damage and long-term disease rather than discrete workplace injuries, addressing chronic conditions and lifestyle risk factors.
health protocols.context: Health is, first, about avoiding cumulative, irreparable damage. Having a pet rattlesnake is unsafe. Working a stressful job that drives you to smoke is unhealthy.

tinkering (protocol design).definition: The intentional, incremental modification of existing protocols by adding or adjusting specific steps, characterized by moderate speed and magnitude of change relative to design or error-based mutation.
tinkering (protocol design).context: To tinker is to intentionally mutate a protocol in some way. For example, one could add a step to a workplace inspection checklist. The pace of mutation by tinkering is likely slower than by memetic error. But it is faster and less dramatic than protocol design.

protocol design.definition: The intentional creation or comprehensive redesign of protocols to be substantially different from existing protocols, characterized by the strongest magnitude of mutation but high risk of rejection if too radical.
protocol design.context: Protocol design, which is creating or changing a protocol so that it is unique from existing protocols. The strength of mutations from design easily places protocols into the realm of infeasibility, where actors will reject them.

protocol atrophy.definition: The gradual decline and death of a protocol through disuse when it is no longer actively performed or reinforced by the social network.
protocol atrophy.context: Like muscles, without use, a protocol atrophies; for a protocol to die, it needs only to not be used.

hazard creation (sources).definition: The three primary drivers that generate new workplace dangers: environmental change, technological progress including knowledge, and shifts in the social order and power distribution.
hazard creation (sources).context: New protocols emerge when we encounter newly created hazards. There are three sources of hazard creation. The first source of hazard creation in the model is environmental change... The second source of hazard creation is technological progress... The third source of hazard creation is change in the social order.

latency period.definition: The delayed interval between occupational exposure to a hazard (such as asbestos) and the clinical manifestation of disease, complicating causal attribution and health protocol development.
latency period.context: causality is difficult to prove given the long timespan between exposure and disease (for example, asbestosis has a latency period of 15 to 30 years), and a mechanism of harm is often below the level of human perception.

protocolized.definition: The process or state in which protocol participants internalize protocols so deeply that they become unconscious inhabitants of infrastructures, their dispositions and agency obscured by the systems they inhabit.
protocolized.context: Among them, she identifies a particularly tough problem — that of protocol participants internalizing protocols and becoming "protocolized" themselves, turning into unconscious inhabitants of infrastructures whose dispositions they cannot quite see.
protocolized.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

protocol as medium.definition: The concept that protocols function as formative technological mediums that shape human behavior, consciousness, and social relations, producing new kinds of humans and new forms of human agency.
protocol as medium.context: For better or worse, the medium is the message, and new sorts of humans are the message of protocols.
protocol as medium.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

legibility tradeoff.definition: The fundamental tension in protocol design where solutions to platform problems reproduce difficult tradeoffs but in less transparent or legible forms, making the consequences harder to perceive and address.
legibility tradeoff.context: protocols are no panacea for the ills of a world of platforms; they merely reproduce many of the fundamentally difficult tradeoffs in newer, less legible forms.
legibility tradeoff.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

phenomenology of protocols.definition: The study of how protocols are subjectively experienced, perceived, and lived through by participants, examining consciousness, moral agency, and the felt dimensions of protocol participation.
phenomenology of protocols.context: Janna takes a meditative look at danger and safety through the lenses of morality, agency, flourishing, and conviviality.
phenomenology of protocols.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

praxis of protocols.definition: A lived and livable philosophy of protocols that integrates both theoretical understanding and practical wisdom about how to design, inhabit, and adapt protocols for human flourishing.
praxis of protocols.context: What we have in this set of essays may be the beginnings of an entire praxis of protocols; a lived (and livable) philosophy of protocols.
praxis of protocols.source: Protocol Kit Package 3: Danger and Safety (editorial framing)

inhabiting protocols.definition: The active process of living within and operationalizing a protocol system, transforming abstract rules into lived social practice.
inhabiting protocols.context: both explore the social processes of inhabiting protocols, turning systems of rules and automation into living, breathing entities
inhabiting protocols.source: Summer of Protocols Kit - Mailer 4 (Social Science of Protocols)

protocolized economics.definition: Economic systems and practices that have been formalized into explicit protocol structures governing exchange, coordination, and value distribution.
protocolized economics.context: Supporting these essays, we have a short piece by Steve Powers called Protocolized Economics
protocolized economics.source: Summer of Protocols Kit - Mailer 4 (Social Science of Protocols)

killswitch protocols.definition: Governance mechanisms that function as overrides or failsafes to prevent unchecked execution of system procedures and ensure distributed authority, ranging from fully automated to entirely human-driven.
killswitch protocols.context: Killswitch governance protocols can range from fully automated to entirely human-driven and from centralized to distributed, and feature a wide range of costs and benefits. In a world whose organizational processes are increasingly automated and distributed, killswitches are increasingly central to protocol design due to their role in ensuring true distribution of governance authority.

worlds.definition: Communities or ecosystems that grow on a protocol when a protocol lives, including games, social media platforms, and other communal spaces that can have mortality and require archiving.
worlds.context: Worlds are what grows on a protocol when a protocol lives, though they can grow on other substrates, including games, social media platforms, and other communal spaces. The core thesis of this essay is that the death of a world is a decision-making process with a duration, rather than an atomic event.

swarm.definition: A networked collective of people, bots, and content coordinated through algorithmic feedback loops without explicit coordination protocols, capable of collective action through minimal protocolization.
swarm.context: On the internet, we are part of swarms: networks of people, bots, and content, coordinated through algorithmic feedback loops. Swarms are networked tempests of humans and information. Most importantly, they can act collectively without explicit coordination protocols; they are minimally protocolized entities.

formation.definition: A group such as memetic tribes or online communities that possess explicit protocols shaping collective action, distinguishing them from swarms which lack such formal coordination mechanisms.
formation.context: We also contrast swarms with their natural online complement: formations. Formations are groups like memetic tribes and online communities that do have explicit protocols shaping collective action, distinguishing them from swarms.

alignment technologies.definition: Technologies and methods used to orient a collective or swarm toward unified action and shared objectives.
alignment technologies.context: The project explores the network technologies that sustained the formation and the alignment technologies that oriented the swarm toward collective action.
alignment technologies.source: The Swarm Effect: China's 2022 Covid Protests

timekeeping protocols.definition: Systems and devices that regulate the measurement and experience of time, functioning as sites of control and power that shape consciousness and social organization.
timekeeping protocols.context: Timekeeping protocols, and the devices they are intertwined with, have shaped consciousness and been a primary site of control and power throughout history.

artificial memory.definition: The use of external or internal aids to extend and systematize human remembering, including techniques like mnemonics, songlines, and digital archives that help preserve and retrieve information beyond natural memory capacity.
artificial memory.context: In contrast to the idea of natural memory, artificial memory involves using aids to help us remember. These include internal aids like memorization techniques that enrich personal memory and external aids like encyclopedias that enrich societal memory.

memory protocols.definition: Systematic approaches and practices designed to help individuals and communities orient in their narratives and curate collective lore through organized memory practices.
memory protocols.context: Memory protocols are not just about storage and recitation. They matter because they help us orient in the seas of our stories—they help us curate the collective lore that glues communities together.

protocol monopoly.definition: A situation where one protocol design dominates a market so completely that competing platforms must adopt the same core mechanics to remain viable, leaving users with no meaningful alternative.
protocol monopoly.context: Swiping now occupies a dysfunctional 'protocol monopoly'... The apps outside of Match Group (e.g., Bumble, Coffee Meets Bagel) must also submit to the monopoly form (swipe protocols) for users to onboard with ease.

protocol system experience.definition: A conceptual framework describing how an individual participant enters, performs a role, and makes decisions within a protocol system, grappling with consciousness, agency, power, and change.
protocol system experience.context: This essay looks at the experience of an individual participant in a protocol system—how they enter, perform a role, and make decisions about their future within (or outside of) it.

protocolized governance.definition: A system of coordinated decision-making and resource management organized through formal, documented, and iteratively refined protocols that balance global coordination with local autonomy.
protocolized governance.context: While the city has found that protocolized governance works for them, it is largely dependent on two things: trust between neighbors and neighborhoods and consistent and expansive public engagement.

method of loci.definition: An ancient memorization technique in which facts and images are mentally associated with specific locations within an imagined formal structure, allowing systematic mental traversal for recall.
method of loci.context: This technique of memorization, where facts are associated with specific locations, later became known as the method of loci. The procedure involved selecting a 'formal structure,' be it a cherished church, school, or home, and within that formal structure, designating distinct 'memory places.'

protocol friction.definition: The tension or misalignment between protocols and the systems they govern, where rigid base layer infrastructure cannot adapt quickly enough to changing demands and uses.
protocol friction.context: Traffic congestion is a representative problem of the contemporary Western city: a chronic tension between the built environment's hard constraints and the fluid, volatile demand for that infrastructure.

pace layers.definition: Stewart Brand's framework that distinguishes different layers of environmental change operating at different timescales, from fast-moving furniture to slow-moving infrastructure, each of which different parties can engage with as participants.
pace layers.context: Stewart Brand's pace layers, again, illustrate the variable nature of environmental agency: Various protocol layers act as surfaces with which different parties can engage as participants. Some of us can only modify the top layers—rearranging the furniture in our homes, literally or figuratively—while others have the ability to change the base layers, such as the building's structure or even the site on which it sits.
pace layers.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

shearing.definition: The dynamic tension between different pace layers of a system as they change at different rates, creating friction when slow systems block fast ones and vice versa.
shearing.context: The tension or 'shearing' between the built environment's various layers as they change at different rates is an unavoidable condition, but Brand notes that an adaptive system allows for 'slippage' between those layers.

infrastructure space.definition: The immaterial, invisible layer of powerful activities and information systems that govern how objects and content are organized and circulated in the physical realm.
infrastructure space.context: The information resides in invisible, powerful activities that determine how objects and content are organized and circulated.

permissionless urbanism.definition: Urban development and settlement patterns that emerge without formal planning or official permission, often occurring in informal settlements on city margins.
permissionless urbanism.context: The same is true of the massive informal settlements that have flourished on the margins of cities around the world: permissionless urbanism for populations who can't access the official version.

protocol failure.definition: When a protocol fails to achieve its internal objectives or when it succeeds internally while producing negative externalities or missing opportunities at larger scales.
protocol failure.context: When a protocol fails, it does not fail according to external criteria, but according to its own internal objectives.

positive mode (of protocol failure).definition: A type of protocol failure that creates tangible, visible problems such as congestion, waste accumulation, or rising costs.
positive mode (of protocol failure).context: The positive mode creates a tangible problem—garbage piling up on the street, traffic congestion, rising housing costs, crime.

negative mode (of protocol failure).definition: A type of protocol failure consisting of missed opportunities, unrealized transactions, and uncreated value that are difficult to observe or quantify.
negative mode (of protocol failure).context: The negative mode, however, consists of missed opportunity: the markets that weren't made, the transactions that didn't occur, the value not created.

infrastructural fatalism.definition: A resigned acceptance that chronic infrastructure problems like traffic congestion are inevitable and unresolvable, treated as natural features to plan around rather than problems to solve.
infrastructural fatalism.context: Despite the looming prospect of self-driving cars finally rationalizing traffic, most drivers do not expect congestion to go away; our acceptance of the traffic jam is a kind of infrastructural fatalism.

slippage.definition: The adaptive space between different pace layers of a system that allows quick-changing elements to innovate without tearing up slow systems, preventing them from blocking each other.
slippage.context: An adaptive system allows for 'slippage' between those layers: Otherwise the slow systems block the flow of the quick ones, and the quick ones tear up the slow ones with their constant change.

coordination mechanism.definition: A set of rules, norms, incentives, and design affordances that translate potentially chaotic behavior into more orderly collective outcomes toward shared goals.
coordination mechanism.context: Broadly, protocols can be understood as infrastructure plus behavior (this oversimplifies the concept somewhat but will suffice for now).

protocol nesting.definition: The organizational structure where protocols are frequently embedded within other protocols at multiple scales, from local to global, with nested protocols forming complex systems.
protocol nesting.context: If the city itself is a protocol, it is also a Russian doll that comprises many more protocols, at every scale. That is, protocols are frequently nested within other protocols, in the built environment and everywhere else.

induced demand.definition: The phenomenon where increasing the capacity of infrastructure (such as roads) leads to increased usage that eventually returns the system to similar congestion levels.
induced demand.context: Traffic congestion is notorious for being a problem you cannot simply build your way out of. Expanding highway capacity induces additional demand following a period of temporary relief, ultimately settling at a new equilibrium that is as bad as the original congestion.

gizmo.definition: A small, self-contained unit of high performance that functions as a clip-on device, characterized by versatility and portability that enhances broader systems.
gizmo.context: In his 1965 essay 'The Great Gizmo,' Reyner Banham praised the potent role of the gizmo or 'clip-on device' in American culture, which he describes as 'a small self-contained unit of high performance in relation to its size and cost.'

externalities.definition: Costs or responsibilities typically borne by employers that are instead transferred to the public realm and other parties, creating problems in shared spaces that others must address.
externalities.context: Third-party delivery platforms like Uber and DoorDash minimize costs by avoiding responsibilities and costs that employers typically bear on behalf of their employees. Many of these costs are not eliminated but externalized, transferred to the public realm where they create problems that others must deal with.
externalities.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

urbanist's dilemma.definition: The fundamental problem that urban planners cannot adequately shape the built environment through physical design alone, as protocols and global forces beyond their control dominate contemporary urbanism.
urbanist's dilemma.context: The contemporary urbanist is stifled by protocols, having failed to adequately recognize or engage with them. 'Architects and designers stick to the discrete and the designable,' Albert Pope writes, 'even as their efforts are undermined by forces far beyond their control.'

junkspace.definition: Large expanses of contemporary built environment characterized by illegibility and disorientation, including suburban sprawl, shopping malls, airports, and office buildings that supplant more legible urban forms like the rectilinear grid.
junkspace.context: An ever-expanding landscape of suburban sprawl, shopping malls, airports, and office buildings—what Marc Augé called "non-places" and Rem Koolhaas called "junkspace"—continues to supplant the more legible forms of urban fabric that preceded it, such as the rectilinear grid.

enabling field.definition: A type of urban infrastructure or protocol design that creates conditions for diverse processes and unforeseen opportunities rather than forcing predetermined outcomes.
enabling field.context: It will no longer aim for stable configurations but for the creation of enabling fields that accommodate processes that refuse to be crystallized into definitive form.

protocol monument.definition: Large-scale infrastructure created as a side effect of protocols' functional objectives rather than for commemorative purposes, whose charismatic qualities are incidental to their primary function.
protocol monument.context: Today we build fulfillment centers, freeways, container ships, and supertall skyscrapers, all accidental monuments to the various protocols that utilize them.

immaterial apparatus.definition: The non-physical layer of rules, norms, and coordinating mechanisms that direct and organize behavior within the built environment and information systems.
immaterial apparatus.context: Protocols are the immaterial apparatus that support and direct the physically grounded information flows that are concentrated in cities and transmitted by urban infrastructure.

temporal mismatch.definition: A misalignment between how quickly the built environment can adapt and how rapidly needs, demands, and conditions change, causing systems to become outdated.
temporal mismatch.context: The jam is a temporal mismatch between the supply of road capacity and the demand for it.

spatial mismatch.definition: The geographic disconnect between where benefits accrue and where costs are borne, and between global forces and local control in urban systems.
spatial mismatch.context: The built environment, again, is temporally mismatched to collective needs, it is spatially mismatched: the mechanisms for effecting change at local and individual scales are deficient.

simultaneous enablement and restraint.definition: The dual characteristic of protocols whereby they function as both enabling tools for coordinated action and constraining forces that limit behavior and agency.
simultaneous enablement and restraint.context: Simultaneous enablement and restraint: Protocols possess dual characteristics, acting as both enablers and constraints in various capacities.

inherent temporality.definition: The fundamental quality that protocols exist within and are structured by time; they are intrinsically process-oriented and realized through temporal enactment rather than design alone.
inherent temporality.context: Inherent temporality: Protocols exist within the realm of time; they are intrinsically process-oriented. Where there are protocols, there is temporality; no temporality, no protocols.

emergency brake protocols.definition: Protocols designed to secure or reinstate stable conditions in reaction to perceived threats or crises, introduced within existing frameworks and requiring social or legal legitimation.
emergency brake protocols.context: These emergency brake protocols are designed to secure or reinstate a stable ground in reaction to a perceived threat. They do not necessarily arise post-disaster but are predicated on the anticipation of potential catastrophe, which legitimizes their imposition.

convention-driven (social) protocols.definition: Protocols that emerge from social tradition and repeated practice, appearing self-evident and natural rather than explicitly designed, often transmitted through socialization.
convention-driven (social) protocols.context: Convention-driven (social) protocols, a second category, are less overtly provoked by crises; they often appear to be almost 'second nature' and, consequently, timeless. Handshakes and roles within family or professional contexts are often just 'how things are done.'

optimization-driven protocols.definition: Protocols at the intersection of technological and social realms designed to improve efficiency and coordination, including traffic regulation, standards-making, and formal organizational rules.
optimization-driven protocols.context: Optimization-driven protocols, as a third category, sit at the intersection of the technological realm and the social sphere. Examples include traffic regulation, standards-making processes, the rules of formal organizations, and perhaps even web development tools.

weakly expressed protocols.definition: Protocols that are implicit, unconscious, or poorly articulated, making them difficult to examine or alter because their designed and strategic nature has been obscured through repeated practice.
weakly expressed protocols.context: Nadia Asparouhova refers to weakly expressed protocols. Only when such protocols become conscious or 'strongly expressed' can they be altered.

strongly expressed protocols.definition: Protocols that are conscious, explicit, and clearly articulated, making them susceptible to deliberate alteration and reflection by participants.
strongly expressed protocols.context: Only when such protocols become conscious or 'strongly expressed' can they be altered. For example, the handshake, deeply internalized as a hallmark of 'western-style' decorum, was overridden by the emergency protocol of social distancing.

circular temporality.definition: The temporal structure of protocol enactment characterized by perfect or near-perfect reproduction of prescribed action across repeated cycles, with minimal variation or evolution.
circular temporality.context: The circle represents a perfect reproduction of action according to protocol, while the spiral illustrates a gradual shift, an evolution of the protocol through its enactment. Handshakes are an example of the former.

spiral temporality.definition: The temporal structure of protocol enactment where repetitive cycles gradually shift and evolve, with each iteration containing variation that enables slow but sustained change without exact duplication.
spiral temporality.context: I propose that this midpoint of the evolutionary process in optimization-driven technological or organizational protocols can be best visualized as a spiral temporality, both circularly repetitive and somewhat linear, where no repetition is an exact replica of the previous one.

loose coupling.definition: A relationship between protocol and participant that allows flexibility and conscious choice, enabling gradual evolution while maintaining enough structure for coordination.
loose coupling.context: When participation is conscious (but hence also optional) and allows for flexibility, a loose coupling between protocol and actor, protocolization can facilitate slow but steady evolution.

second nature.definition: The state in which protocols become so deeply internalized and habituated that their designed nature is hidden and they appear as natural, inevitable ways of acting.
second nature.context: Protocols hence contain contradictory tendencies—of dynamic change and evolution on the one hand, and of routinization and conservation on the other... become so internalized that they appear as 'second nature,' deeply ingrained within individuals' behavior.

teleology.definition: In protocol analysis, the vision of a future end-state or 'beyond-protocol' condition toward which a protocol is oriented.
teleology.context: • the teleology of their protocols, or the vision of a 'beyond'-protocol future state

figure-ground relationship.definition: An analytical framework in which protocols are understood as distinct entities with defined boundaries that either emerge from or are built upon a foundational environment, while remaining distinguishable from it.
figure-ground relationship.context: The perspective of this analysis operates under the assumption that protocols can be envisioned using a figure-ground relationship. Protocols are distinct entities with defined boundaries that either emerge from or are built upon a foundational ground, an environment.

crisis threat.definition: The condition of heightened uncertainty or danger that motivates the emergence and design of protocols as responsive mechanisms.
crisis threat.context: I argue that all these types of protocols arise out of or are a functional response to crises or the threat of it, creating significant uncertainties in an environment.

means-before-ends.definition: A characterization of protocols that emphasize coordination mechanisms and routinized procedures over articulated goals or future visions.
means-before-ends.context: In other words, protocols are means of solving problems of the past and present in the future without actually having an inspired vision of the future or an end-goal... the means themselves may become the ends as social actors lose sight of the problems or crises of the past that the protocols were supposed to address.

minimally protocolized.definition: Entities or systems that lack explicit, formally stated protocols and instead rely on external algorithms and emergent coordination for alignment.
minimally protocolized.context: Most importantly, they can act collectively without explicit protocols; they are minimally protocolized entities.

emergency time.definition: Moments characterized by rapid acceleration of action and sense-making processes, where conditions reach critical points and require urgent coordination and response.
emergency time.context: Specifically, I will conclude by offering a succinct reflection on the role of protocols in the context of unfolding global climate change... moments characterized by a rapid acceleration of action and sense-making processes.

routinization.definition: The process by which protocols become habitual and standardized through repeated enactment, making them appear natural and reducing conscious reflection on their design.
routinization.context: Importantly, some degree of internalization is still essential to sustain participation. The benefit of protocols only comes with routinization, a streamlining of repetitive action that exemplarily illustrates the duality of enabling and constraining effects.

innovation-preservation axis.definition: The spectrum along which protocols are oriented, with some leaning toward changing environments (innovation-driven) and others toward maintaining existing conditions (preservation-oriented).
innovation-preservation axis.context: • the innovative or preserving intentions of their protocols, that is, their fundamental orientation toward future or past

tiring effects.definition: The exhausting impact on protocol participants caused by sustained adherence to rules, particularly emergency-driven protocols that strain social actors over prolonged periods.
tiring effects.context: While some long-term effects of COVID-19 protocols remain to be determined, it's evident from this case that we do not fully understand the internalization of a protocol as a process... COVID-19 regulations exhibited tiring effects on many individuals.

uptake.definition: The adoption and practical enactment of protocols by social actors; the process through which protocols come to life through actual participation.
uptake.context: This is what weds protocols to time. Protocols come to life in their execution, that is, in their uptake by participants.

standard.definition: An agreed-upon measurement, term, or rule that establishes trust between engineers and enables commerce, industry, and technological possibilities.
standard.context: For the purposes of this essay, standards refer to the spec and standards-making to the process.

standards-making.definition: The dynamic process by which groups of people create, refine, and implement standards, evolving over time through different organizational models and approaches.
standards-making.context: Standards are not divine rights. They are made and remade by (usually small) groups of people and projected into the world through various means and with varying effectiveness. And that process is dynamic.

standardization entrepreneurs.definition: Visionary individuals who convene and build consensus amongst engineers and organizations to establish new standards, often volunteering their expertise for the public good.
standardization entrepreneurs.context: Support of technical standardization coalesced into a recognizable social movement by the 1920s. Standards entrepreneurs like Charles Le Maestre, head of the British Engineering Standards Association, gained status and influence through their commitment to the common project.

safety standards.definition: Standards designed to prevent harm and protect public welfare through specifications for design, construction, and maintenance of technologies and infrastructure.
safety standards.context: Exploding steam boilers on riverboats caused engineers and policymakers to rally around standards for design, construction, and maintenance.

interoperability standards.definition: Standards that ensure different components or systems from different manufacturers can work together seamlessly.
interoperability standards.context: Screw threads were a matter of obvious convenience; standard designs would make lost screws easily replaceable by local shops.

performance standards.definition: Industry-wide assurances of quality that allow manufacturers to quantify durability and justify value propositions, facilitating commerce.
performance standards.context: Steel manufacturers needed a way to quantify their durability and justify higher prices over iron rails, but they didn't have an easy way to convince buyers. Performance standards—industry-wide assurances of quality—helped facilitate commerce.

first wave (of standards-making).definition: The earliest major standards movement (1880s-1920s) where interested parties made cases for shared designs and convinced others to join through informal working groups.
first wave (of standards-making).context: The first wave occurred between the 1880s and 1920s. The standards-making process was mostly straightforward, mimicking what worked for Sellers and Whitworth: groups of interested parties made the case for a shared design and convinced others to join.

second wave (of standards-making).definition: The post-WWII standards movement (1960s-1980s) characterized by globalization, transnational adoption, and the rise of international organizations like ISO.
second wave (of standards-making).context: By the 1950s, the second wave had started and thrived between the 1960s and 1980s. Globalization was the story, and associations like the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) were formed to facilitate transnational adoption.

third wave (of standards-making).definition: The computer era standards movement where consortium models and disruptive approaches emerged to keep pace with rapid innovation.
third wave (of standards-making).context: The third wave of standards entrepreneurs grew alongside the development of computers and computer networking. As engineers and companies quickly innovated, the need for standards outpaced the capacity of the international, multi-stakeholder consensus process, and another model emerged in response.

consortium model.definition: A standards-making approach where the parties most closely involved in development (companies, engineers, etc.) self-organize to create standards for their specific purposes.
consortium model.context: Yates and Murphy called this a 'consortium' model, where the parties most closely involved in development (companies, engineers, etc.) self-organized to create standards that worked for their purposes.

commercial diplomacy.definition: The strategic use of standards control and negotiation by technology companies to induce network effects and win market share.
commercial diplomacy.context: Technology companies compete to control standards in order to induce network effects and win market share. Stephen Walli refers to this as the art of 'commercial diplomacy.'

de facto standards.definition: Standards that emerge from market dominance by a single actor, where competitors adopt the standard because of its established market position.
de facto standards.context: Tesla raced ahead to fill the market need, earning the right to set the spec, and now even their most ardent competitors are falling in line. It's classic de facto standards-making.

disruptive standards-making.definition: A standards approach where upstart outsiders develop working implementations first and gain market adoption before formalizing through official standards bodies, resembling Clayton Christensen's disruptive innovation model.
disruptive standards-making.context: I call the process 'disruptive standards-making' because of the close resemblance to Clayton Christensen's model of disruptive innovation where unassuming outsiders break through with fast-improving technology.

rough consensus and running code.definition: A standards-making principle emphasizing that practical working implementations and general agreement matter more than formal consensus procedures.
rough consensus and running code.context: David Clark's famous address to the IETF in 1992, 'A Cloudy Crystal Ball,' is remembered for the defiant credo of 'rough consensus and running code.'

arpanet.definition: The precursor network to the Internet, developed by DARPA as a practical solution for connecting different packet technologies, which pioneered disruptive standards-making approaches.
arpanet.context: The Internet Protocol was the pioneering disruptive standard, even though DARPA didn't set out to create a new type of standards-making process. The ARPANET program was meant to solve a practical problem in the cheapest way possible.

internet engineering task force (ietf).definition: The group responsible for managing Internet protocols and standards, pioneering a new model of disruptive standards-making based on rough consensus and working implementations.
internet engineering task force (ietf).context: Even the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the group responsible for managing the nascent Internet protocol, recognized the moment.

open source software.definition: Software where the source code is publicly available and developers can freely contribute, fork, and improve, representing a full standards movement based on permissionless innovation.
open source software.context: The rise of open source software represents a full-on standards movement. Engineers build reputations through their contributions to the commons in the same way that the early standards entrepreneurs would gain status for their efforts.

hacker culture.definition: A culture that emerged around open source software and early computing, characterized by an ethic of sharing, permissionlessness, and solving problems without seeking prior approval.
hacker culture.context: The first intentional artifacts of the hacker culture—the first slang lists, the first satires, the first self-conscious discussions of the hacker ethic—all propagated on the ARPAnet in its early years.

permissionlessness.definition: An approach to standards development where participants proceed to implement and contribute without requiring approval from formal authorities or existing standards bodies.
permissionlessness.context: Few open source developers seek approval before getting started. They see a need and proceed to fill it, whether by contributing to an existing codebase or starting anew, regardless if they are actively rebelling against legacy standards-making processes or blissfully unaware.

market fit.definition: In standards-making, the successful adoption and implementation of a standard in the market, analogous to product-market fit in startup contexts.
market fit.context: Startups know they need product/market fit in order for their companies to be successful. Standardizers, too, must find market fit in order to survive.

failure to launch.definition: A critical failure mode in standards-making where a potential standardizing effort stalls at the pre-conceptualization stage due to lack of sponsorship, vision, or opposition.
failure to launch.context: The first is on the front end: a failure to launch a potential standardizing effort. Any number of problems can stall a project at this pre-conceptualization stage: a lack of enthusiasm from potential sponsors, the originator lacking charisma and vision, or even fear of antitrust or anti-competition accusations from market players.

bristlemouth.definition: A standardized interface and protocol for modular underwater vehicle components, designed to enable interoperability and innovation in autonomous underwater vehicles.
bristlemouth.context: Every component is its own modular part, and they're all connected through a standardized interface which we're calling Bristlemouth.

open source hardware.definition: Hardware designs, specifications, and source files made publicly available for modification and reuse, attempting to apply open source software principles to physical devices.
open source hardware.context: There have been valiant attempts to create an open source hardware movement—and the Bristlemouth team were an active part of that in the early days—but it's remained niche.

populist paradigm.definition: A contested theoretical framework or worldview that gains widespread popular and internet-driven adoption while existing largely outside institutional scientific validation, presenting challenges to traditional knowledge protocols.
populist paradigm.context: These 'populist paradigms,' to twist Thomas Kuhn's term, present a dual challenge. On the one hand, they obviously have spread largely outside the university, bypassing and thus failing to meet the rigorous standards for adjudication that typically accompany scientific claims.

paradigm refugee.definition: A researcher forced to abandon their original research focus because they were systematically excluded from grants and publishing opportunities by a dominant paradigm hostile to their theoretical approach.
paradigm refugee.context: The decades-long silent embargo forced some researchers to pivot to other topics, creating a class of 'paradigm refugees' unable to continue their original work in a hostile environment.

paradigm shift.definition: A fundamental change in the dominant theoretical framework and methods of a scientific discipline, occurring when sufficient anomalies accumulate to make a new explanatory model more compelling than the prevailing one.
paradigm shift.context: If enough of these anomalies accrue, it's possible for new, non-paradigm hypotheses to gain attention in the scientific community and cause a paradigm shift.

broscience.definition: Informal, experiential knowledge about fitness and health produced and shared by bodybuilders and fitness enthusiasts, typically based on personal experimentation rather than formal scientific validation.
broscience.context: Terminally online conservatives have picked up the importance of the endocrine system from testosterone-maxing bodybuilders, whose 'broscience' is informed by nootropics and supplement experimenters who themselves are in dialogue with credentialed vitamin researchers.

crystallize.definition: The process by which knowledge protocols emerge and take solid form in response to information-saturated environments requiring new organizing structures.
crystallize.context: It seems that these protocols tend to appear, or perhaps 'crystallize,' in environments supersaturated with information.

seed oil sophistry.definition: The use of selective interpretation of scientific evidence and rhetorical techniques to support claims about the harms of seed oils, characterized by flawed reasoning and cherry-picking studies.
seed oil sophistry.context: A Patreon-supported nutritional science blogger who goes by The Nutrivore has written an extensive critique of what he calls 'seed oil sophistry'...

participatory public health moonshot.definition: An ambitious, large-scale public health research initiative designed to integrate amateur scientists and online communities into the experimental design and data collection process.
participatory public health moonshot.context: This sort of participatory public health moonshot is exactly the sort of experiment needed to build consensus and resolve the institutional distrust that plagues our medical system.

global spasm of participatory science.definition: A rapid, coordinated, and distributed worldwide effort by scientists and amateurs to replicate and test hypotheses through internet-enabled collaboration and real-time documentation.
global spasm of participatory science.context: More importantly, Tim Hwang reflects, the phenomenon can claim success not only in terms of growing public awareness, but as the internet making possible a 'global spasm of participatory science.'

amyloid hypothesis.definition: The dominant scientific paradigm in Alzheimer's research positing that accumulation of amyloid-beta protein is the primary cause of the disease, which has resisted alternative theoretical approaches.
amyloid hypothesis.context: This is clearly visible in Alzheimer's research, where scientists working outside the predominant amyloid hypothesis were systematically excluded from grants and publishing opportunities.

paradigm-shifting work.definition: Research efforts that challenge and potentially overturn the dominant theoretical framework of a scientific field, as opposed to incremental research that operates within an established paradigm.
paradigm-shifting work.context: The information citizen science gathers and makes fact is already theoretically predicted or only needs crowdsourced confirmation. Research efforts to understand animal migratory patterns or weather systems are examples of necessary, but not paradigm-shifting work.

trusted intermediary.definition: An institutional or procedural mechanism that allows credibility and trust to be transferred from individuals to standardized systems of verification and publication.
trusted intermediary.context: The new interface of journals enabled that person-to-person trust to be offloaded onto a standardized—protocolized—procedure.

algorithmic coordination.definition: The process by which algorithms, rather than explicit rules or central planning, coordinate the actions and attention of networked participants.
algorithmic coordination.context: Unlike traditional organizations, swarms rely on algorithms for coordination instead of uniform social protocols like planning processes, approvals, and chain-of-command.
