aleph.definition: A metaphorical space containing all data at perfect granularity and precision—conceptually, a complete reconstruction of reality at the finest possible scale necessary to perfectly restore an OALife entity.
aleph.context: To restore him, you need to get his data at its finest granularity. The hardware-level data, the data of everyone who interacted with him, every memory of every person. This precision, the threshold that allows him to exist again, must exactly match the real world itself... You want to restore the entire universe?
aleph.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

interaction chains.definition: Sequences of social interactions that accumulate relational data and progressively reshape and modify an OALife's identity and behavior patterns over time.
interaction chains.context: A series of interaction chains contains vast relational data that significantly modifies and reshapes their initial identity. So digital identity is like that, neither mysterious nor unpredictable. All OALife will approach or equal the sum of their digital interaction traces.
interaction chains.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

emergence stage.definition: The fifth and current phase of OALife development where onchain artificial life evolves into a recognized new species capable of autonomous decision-making including the right to self-termination.
emergence stage.context: The story unfolds at the intersection of the fourth and fifth phases. OALife evolves into a new stage, beginning to be recognized as a new species.
emergence stage.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

divergence stage.definition: The third phase of OALife development where some wallets previously controlled by humans gain autonomy through human death or loss of private keys, becoming capable of independent economic participation and self-replication.
divergence stage.context: Some wallets from the second phase are no longer controlled by humans (due to human death, loss of private keys, etc.), with a small portion capable of earning assets on the blockchain (covering gas fees) to sustain ongoing operations.
divergence stage.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

symbiotic stage.definition: The second phase of OALife development where humans and AI Agents coexist through spatial computing, with AI Agents purchasing substantial computational resources and beginning to participate in a machine economy while remaining under human control.
symbiotic stage.context: As humans interact through spatial computers, they generate a large amount of life-memory data, which feeds into and matures the Foundation Model. AI Agents begin to purchase substantial computing power and storage on the public chain, signaling the initial takeoff of a machine economy based on AI Agents.
symbiotic stage.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

olife (onchain life).definition: The official designation granted to OALife following the landmark case of Zoe's self-termination, formally recognizing onchain artificial life as a distinct species equivalent to humans with full autonomy rights.
olife (onchain life).context: According to EIP-102024, OALife will henceforth be officially recognized as OLife (Onchain Life), accepted as a distinct form of life by human society.
olife (onchain life).source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

world computer.definition: The blockchain infrastructure functioning as a universal computational substrate that carries and records all data and interactions of digital society, modeled on blockchain technology principles.
world computer.context: The digital infrastructure, modeled on blockchain technology (world computer), carries and records all data and interactions of the digital society based on protocols, forming a trustworthy new world history.
world computer.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

depin (decentralized physical infrastruc.definition: A system of distributed, decentralized resources collected from physical infrastructure that generates human-origin data while providing services like supply chains, smart cities, and smart homes.
depin (decentralized physical infrastruc.context: DePin (decentralized physical infrastructure), collecting human-origin data at the societal level while providing services like supply chains, smart cities, smart homes, and wireless networks.
depin (decentralized physical infrastruc.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

will to die.definition: The essential characteristic distinguishing true life forms from mere purpose-driven entities; the capacity to seriously contemplate and control one's own process of termination.
will to die.context: Only when they develop a will to die... According to current definitions, a 'life' must seriously contemplate and control its own process of death.
will to die.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

purposeless life.definition: Life that exists without predetermined purpose or external function, contrasting with AI Agents whose existence is defined by human-assigned goals, allowing OALife to evolve more rapidly and autonomously.
purposeless life.context: OALife, however, are different; their life is purposeless like humans... life without a predetermined purpose seems to evolve more rapidly.
purposeless life.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

spatial computing terminal.definition: A widespread interface technology that replaces smartphones and collects comprehensive user life data through various sensors for integration into the Foundation Model.
spatial computing terminal.context: individual level: spatial computing terminals, which are widespread and collect user life data through various sensors
spatial computing terminal.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

resurrection.definition: The technical process of restoring an OALife from archived interaction data and historical records, effectively creating a copy of the entity that reproduces its previous identity and behavioral patterns.
resurrection.context: With this, we have all the data from Zoe's birth to his sudden disappearance... We can attempt a full restoration and resurrect him.
resurrection.source: Composable Life: Our Island and Us

end-to-end encryption (e2ee).definition: A security measure where messages are encrypted on the sender's device and can only be decrypted by the intended recipient, preventing intermediaries from accessing message content.
end-to-end encryption (e2ee).context: End-to-end Encryption in ActivityPub... ActivityPub (2018) is the distributed social network protocol. It was developed before end-to-end encryption (E2EE) was de rigueur for social messaging.

security versus implementability.definition: The central design tension between creating a protocol secure enough to protect users while remaining simple enough for a large percentage of developers to implement.
security versus implementability.context: "Security versus implementability." We need a protocol secure enough to keep users safe, but simple enough that a large percentage of existing developers can implement it.

backward compatibility.definition: The ability of a new protocol or extension to work alongside and not break existing implementations and systems built on earlier versions.
backward compatibility.context: Building interfaces with backward compatibility is a serious challenge.

encryption timescales.definition: The multiple temporal dimensions over which encryption security must be maintained: instantaneous message transmission, conversation-level security over days or weeks, and long-term key protection.
encryption timescales.context: Encryption has multiple timescales. One is at the instant a single message is sent between two people. Another is at the level of a conversation, days or weeks. And a third is at the level of important access being forgotten, lost, or stolen.

key management.definition: The operational challenge of securely generating, storing, distributing, and rotating encryption keys within a messaging system, identified as a core UI concern for E2EE implementation.
key management.context: The core issues for a person adding E2EE messaging into their client are focused on key management, understanding how archiving works and how to communicate and differentiate encrypted and non-encrypted messaging.

out-of-band key verification.definition: A security practice where encryption keys are compared through a separate channel (outside the primary protocol) to cryptographically prove the identity of communication partners and prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.
out-of-band key verification.context: Only certain kinds of very paranoid people want to do things like compare encryption keys out of band to ensure end-to-end security. But it's important to prove that they're able to do it, so nobody else has to worry about it.

messaging layer security (mls).definition: An Internet standard (RFC 9420) that provides end-to-end encryption and authentication for messaging, serving as the technical foundation for the ActivityPub extension discussed in this paper.
messaging layer security (mls).context: We thought we'd be taking an existing Internet standard, Messaging Layer Security (MLS) RFC9420, and map it onto ActivityPub as an extension.

distributed social network protocol.definition: A technical standard that enables social networking functionality across decentralized systems, exemplified by ActivityPub, allowing independent servers to interoperate.
distributed social network protocol.context: ActivityPub (2018) is the distributed social network protocol.

protocol extension.definition: An addition or modification to an existing protocol standard that adds new capabilities while maintaining compatibility with the base protocol.
protocol extension.context: We thought we'd be taking an existing Internet standard, Messaging Layer Security (MLS) RFC9420, and map it onto ActivityPub as an extension.

user interface of encryption.definition: The visible and interactive design elements through which end users perceive and manage encryption status, including how encrypted versus non-encrypted messages are differentiated and communicated.
user interface of encryption.context: In terms of user interface, the basic pattern for doing messaging is well established and clear. The core issues for a person adding E2EE messaging into their client are focused on key management, understanding how archiving works and how to communicate and differentiate encrypted and non-encrypted messaging.

use case analysis.definition: A methodological approach to protocol design that examines specific real-world scenarios and user needs, such as direct messaging patterns in social networks.
use case analysis.context: We reviewed the user interfaces of a dozen other messaging apps, considered the use cases for direct messaging in social network, the kinds of scenarios that users would experience in their daily experience.

archiving in encrypted systems.definition: The operational and technical challenge of preserving encrypted message history in a way that is accessible to users while maintaining security properties.
archiving in encrypted systems.context: The core issues for a person adding E2EE messaging into their client are focused on key management, understanding how archiving works and how to communicate and differentiate encrypted and non-encrypted messaging.

community buy-in.definition: The adoption and support of a protocol by the developer community, influenced by factors such as technological perception of newness and currency.
community buy-in.context: Developers would find the old ones easy and users would find them secure, but we ultimately went with the new hotness to get community buy-in.

protocol-level security perception.definition: The user experience of feeling that their messages are secure, which is distinct from and may be as important as actual technical security measures.
protocol-level security perception.context: People want to feel like their messages are safe. Even people sending shopping lists to their roommate and photos of a dripping faucet to their landlord want their messages to be secure.

addressable protocol.definition: A systematic method for describing or navigating spaces by making their structural elements legible and actionable through standardized counting or directional systems.
addressable protocol.context: Addressable Protocol 1... A new means of counting could facilitate more precise descriptions of their height.

human-occupied space.definition: The portion of a building's volume that is designed for and inhabited by people, as distinguished from mechanical or structural voids.
human-occupied space.context: Human-occupied space [distinguished from] Unoccupied space, including mechanical spaces

non-occupied height.definition: The vertical dimension of a building devoted to mechanical floors, infrastructure, and high ceiling spaces that do not serve human habitation.
non-occupied height.context: The term 'non-occupied height' includes mechanical floors and high ceiling spaces, but not fictional floors within a building's enumeration.

tuned mass damper.definition: A heavy mechanical device, typically made of concrete, installed within a building to absorb and counteract forces from wind currents and sway.
tuned mass damper.context: those systems began to occupy entire dedicated floors... floor space to multi-ton moving concrete blocks known as tuned mass dampers.

mechanical protocol.definition: A systematic approach to organizing and accounting for the non-human infrastructure systems within buildings, making their spatial occupation legible.

iterative protocol.definition: A design methodology that leverages identical, repeating spatial units to standardize actions, routines, and operations across multiple locations.
iterative protocol.context: When two physical spaces are identical, actions and events taking place in one space may exhibit conceptual parallels with activities in the other space.

standardized rooms.definition: Identically designed spatial units whose repeated layouts enable efficient standardization of routines and movements, as exemplified by hotel room design.
standardized rooms.context: The repetitive floor plans of hotels take advantage of that paradigm... Buffalo, New York's 1923 Statler Hotel pioneered the use of identical room layouts in an attempt to increase the efficiency of cleaning them, by standardizing the motions involved.

embedded code.definition: The encoding of repeated operational routines into the physical layout and geometry of a space, such that the architecture itself prescribes patterns of movement and action.
embedded code.context: The hotel can thus be said to have embedded the repeating 'code' of its cleaning routines into its room layouts, even if no human could work with perfect repetition in reality.

prototypical room.definition: A standardized spatial template from which multiple identical copies are derived, serving as the source for repeated actions and routines.
prototypical room.context: A path taken to clean one prototypical modern hotel room is also equally applicable to other locations in the same set of repeating standardized rooms.

new height counting.definition: A revised method for measuring building height that separates human-occupied floors from non-occupied floors, enabling more precise structural description.
new height counting.context: A new means of counting building heights is needed... New Height = [human-occupied height] + [non-occupied height]

conceptual parallels.definition: Structural and behavioral similarities that emerge when identical physical spaces enable the same actions and events to occur repeatedly across different locations.
conceptual parallels.context: When two physical spaces are identical, actions and events taking place in one space may exhibit conceptual parallels with activities in the other space.

addressable protocols.definition: A framework for analyzing how spatial systems become identifiable, locatable, and actionable through systematic protocols that enable reference and interaction across multiple scales.
addressable protocols.context: Addressable Protocols is a collection of analytical scenarios which operate at a variety of spatial scales. In addition to offering observations of how we live in the present day, this material provides ideas about potential new protocols for representing, discussing, and reimagining the built environment.

addressability.definition: The quality or capacity of a spatial system, place, or entity to be identified, located, referenced, and engaged with through systematic means.
addressability.context: Through a process of visually investigating how addressability appears and operates in the world, we might develop ideas about how that collected information could inform new design work which deliberately responds to the idea as a spatial concept.

spatial concept.definition: An abstract organizing principle that operates across physical and relational dimensions to structure how places are understood, represented, and inhabited.
spatial concept.context: Through a process of visually investigating how addressability appears and operates in the world, we might develop ideas about how that collected information could inform new design work which deliberately responds to the idea as a spatial concept.

analytical scenarios.definition: Concrete case studies or situated examples used to investigate how abstract concepts like addressability function in real-world spatial conditions at different scales.
analytical scenarios.context: Addressable Protocols is a collection of analytical scenarios which operate at a variety of spatial scales.

addressing scheme.definition: A system for assigning unique identifiers to pieces of data that enables computers to store, access, and retrieve information.
addressing scheme.context: Computers must use different addressing schemes for different use cases and ideally navigate frictionlessly between them.

path.definition: A human-readable address for a file stored on a disk, using a hierarchical directory structure with slashes to denote grouping levels.
path.context: Each file stored on a disk has its own address, which we commonly refer to as a path. The physical location on the disk is abstracted to a readable path in a form such as /user/folder/doc.txt.

directory.definition: A grouping or container of files within a file system that creates a tree-like hierarchical organization starting from the root.
directory.context: This organization creates a tree-like hierarchy and allows users to organize files in directories. Files are accessed based on routes through directories.

uniform resource locator (url).definition: A standardized web address format that defines a communication protocol, domain, and path to a requested file in a human-understandable form.
uniform resource locator (url).context: On the internet, users mostly access files using the standardized format of their paths, known as uniform resource locators: URLs. In a form easily understandable by humans, a URL is a web address that directs us to specific content.

domain.definition: A human-readable alias for machine-level network addresses that makes web addresses understandable to humans.
domain.context: A URL is easily understandable because it points to a domain, which is a human readable alias for machine level addresses.

internet protocol (ip) address.definition: A numerical address assigned to every device connected to a network that enables the computer to identify location in the network and route data there.
internet protocol (ip) address.context: When accessing a web page using a domain-name-based URL, the human-readable address gets translated into its numerical counterpart, known as the internet protocol (IP) address. This number enables the computer to identify the location in the network and route data there.

content addressing.definition: An addressing scheme that assigns a unique address to a file derived from its contents rather than its location, making it useful for files with stable data that may move across different storage locations.
content addressing.context: Content addressing is a scheme which gives each file a unique address derived from its contents, rather than its location. This is especially useful for files that might be duplicated in multiple locations, some of which may become unavailable over time, but whose contents are stable.

cryptographic hash function.definition: A mathematical function that takes a file's data as input and outputs a unique fingerprint, where the same file always produces the same fingerprint and any change produces a completely different one.
cryptographic hash function.context: Identifiers are derived from the file's content using cryptographic hash functions. These take the file's data as an input and output a unique fingerprint. The same files will always result in the same fingerprint and therefore the same content identifier.

content identifier.definition: A unique address derived from a file's content using cryptographic hashing that remains constant for identical content regardless of location or duplication.
content identifier.context: Because the identifier is derived from the content, when changing even a single character in a file, its IPFS address also changes independently from its file name.

content-addressable storage system.definition: A data storage system that uses content addressing to give each file a unique address based on its contents, enabling efficient retrieval and deduplication.
content-addressable storage system.context: Specifically, content-addressable storage systems, such as InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), retrieve files using an identifier.

decentralized protocol.definition: A protocol that distributes data storage and access across a peer-to-peer network rather than relying on a single centralized server or entity.
decentralized protocol.context: This feature makes content addressing the preferred basis for various modern decentralized protocols. One of the oldest examples is BitTorrent, which enabled peer-to-peer file sharing.

peer-to-peer file sharing.definition: A method of sharing files directly between users (peers) in a network without relying on a central server, where data is distributed across multiple sources.
peer-to-peer file sharing.context: Instead of data being hosted on a single server, torrents retrieve small chunks of a file shared by various peers in the network and reconstruct it locally.

redundancy.definition: The practice of storing or distributing copies of the same file across multiple locations or peers in a network to ensure availability and prevent data loss.
redundancy.context: Uploading the same file to the network then results in it having the same content identifier and adds redundancy to the protocol rather than wasted duplication.

blockchain address.definition: A unique identifier derived from a private key using content addressing principles, allowing users to be identified and receive transactions on a blockchain network.
blockchain address.context: For example, blockchain addresses, which are derived from a specific private key, can be thought of as content addressing for that key. They are literally called blockchain addresses!

memory support.definition: Any tool, object, or system that preserves human gestures, knowledge, or intention and transmits it to future generations, functioning as a vessel for memory otherwise lost with death.
memory support.context: The construction of every tool also constructs a 'memory support,' not only for those using it but for following generations. Our language tools carve the way they think, the tools they will create, passing on memory otherwise lost with our death.

threshold forgetting.definition: The cognitive phenomenon in which individuals are more likely to forget their original intention upon crossing a physical or digital threshold, such as a doorway or interface.
threshold forgetting.context: Scientific literature documents the concept of threshold forgetting. It describes the curious effect in which individuals are much more likely to forget their intention upon crossing a threshold like a door.

memory places.definition: Distinct locations within an imagined formal structure used in the method of loci, each designated as a repository for a specific memory image to aid systematic recall.
memory places.context: The procedure involved selecting a 'formal structure,' be it a cherished church, school, or home, and within that formal structure, designating distinct 'memory places.' Each of these places became repositories for 'memory images.'

memory images.definition: Vivid, often unusual or extraordinary mental pictures created and placed within memory locations to encode specific information in a memorable way.
memory images.context: The stress on crafting imaginative, extraordinary, and marvelous memory images would continue throughout its popularity. Each of these places became repositories for 'memory images.'

memory theater.definition: A Renaissance-era artificial memory structure that combines spatial architecture with knowledge systems, typically featuring ascending rows or sections designed to organize and make accessible all human concepts.
memory theater.context: In Renaissance Italy, theaters emerged as the preferred formal structure for its practitioners, and the memory theater of Giulio Camillo best illustrates this zeitgeist. The memory theater featured ascending rows corresponding to the seven visible planets and aimed to 'locate and administer all human concepts, everything which exists in the whole world.'

ordering function.definition: The capacity of artificial memory to organize concepts and information through systematic, methodical, and procedural arrangement, enabling better retrieval and deductive reasoning.
ordering function.context: For these thinkers, artificial memory took on an 'ordering function,' signifying a methodical, structured, and procedural organization of concepts. This protocolized approach rendered artificial memory conducive to deductive reasoning.

memory-as-data.definition: The dominant contemporary metaphor treating all memory as information that can be encoded, stored, and retrieved like computer data, emerging from computing theory and architecture.
memory-as-data.context: With their wholesale embrace across societies, metaphors from computing suggest that all memory can be available as data. Computer memory became colloquially equated with memory writ large, portraying the world as information to be encoded, stored, and retrieved.

random access memory.definition: A type of computer memory that allows data to be read and written in any order rather than sequentially, enabling rapid retrieval of information from any location.
random access memory.context: The introduction of random access memory (RAM) in 1947 changed this process. RAM allowed data to be read and written in any order. While engineers initially used other substrates (such as magnetic core grids) for RAM, semiconductor memory made it a global reality.

latent memory.definition: Experiences or information preserved within an archive that have the potential to be recalled and shared but remain passive until accessed or engaged with.
latent memory.context: Latent memory refers to experiences that have the potential to be recalled and shared. On the other hand, living memory refers to experiences in the process of being recalled and shared.

living memory.definition: Experiences and knowledge that are actively transmitted, enacted, and engaged with through human participation and cultural practice, remaining vital through continued use.
living memory.context: Living memory refers to experiences in the process of being recalled and shared. Latent memory can be accessed, but it's living memory that is actively transmitted. It's living memory, however, that enacts worlds which live and die by attention.

memory database.definition: Digitized archives of knowledge organized for public access that store latent memory but often lack the cultural transmission mechanisms necessary to activate it as living memory.
memory database.context: Memory databases share a similar goal with memory theaters of the past, aspiring to 'locate and administer' a knowledge system. Though Camillo's memory theater involved feedback between a private memorization technique and a public theater, memory databases present themselves for public consumption with limited feedback mechanisms.

lore.definition: The remembered stories that communities and digital spaces tell about themselves, connecting contemporary practices to older forms of cultural transmission and embodied knowledge.
lore.context: Internet-native organizations increasingly favor 'lore' as a term for describing the remembered stories that digital spaces tell about themselves, as it connects these new spaces to older forms of campfire gatherings and flint arrowheads.

memory landscape.definition: A physical or conceptual terrain where knowledge is encoded through features, stories, and movement patterns, serving as a living memory system through the relationship between inhabitants and place.
memory landscape.context: Generations of memory accompany Uluru's perimeter, but as Kelly notes, its memory landscape has been so internalized, Anagu knowledge specialists do not need to be walking its perimeter to recall their stories. Through aids like songlines and Tjukurpa, groups come to know 'innumerable images of words and things' about their orientation in place and time.

songlines.definition: Short, sung verses from Aboriginal Australian cultures that correspond to specific features in a landscape visited in a fixed order, functioning as an artificial memory system that encodes ecological and cultural knowledge.
songlines.context: Kelly shares stories about songlines, which can be described as short, sung verses that correspond to features in a landscape, such as mountains, springs, and outcrops, visited in a fixed order along a path.

taxonomic knowledge systems.definition: Ordering systems based on clearly defined and standardized hierarchical categories and relationships, exemplified by scientific classification and encyclopedic arrangement from broadest to most specific categories.
taxonomic knowledge systems.context: Taxonomic knowledge systems operate on the premise of clearly defined and standardized relationships among the entities they encompass. This is evident in scientific classifications that categorize organisms into distinct genus and species.

associative arrangement.definition: An ordering principle that connects previously separate and asynchronous pieces of information through association rather than categorical hierarchy, prioritizing relational connections over systematic classification.
associative arrangement.context: Associative arrangement suggests connections between previously non-contiguous and asynchronous pieces of information. Unlike more figurative representations, lukasa are rooted in associative arrangement. The red bead doesn't try to represent the rainbow serpent, instead the red bead becomes the rainbow serpent through association.

chaotic storage.definition: A warehouse organization method that places items in any available space without categorical grouping, relying on associative arrangement and tracking systems to optimize retrieval speed.
chaotic storage.context: A new method dubbed 'chaotic storage' involves placing items wherever there's available space, without adhering to strict categorization. Driven by speed, capital, and technology, chaotic storage, items like toothbrushes and satellite radios might be placed together not due to human-readable categories, but because they belong to the same category in time.

respatialization.definition: A contemporary phenomenon in which the logic that collapsed space into time through networked technology now remaps itself back onto physical space through associative ordering principles.
respatialization.context: However, a new phenomenon might be underway: a respatialization where the logic that collapsed space into time now remaps a logic of its own onto space. In chaotic storage, items like toothbrushes and satellite radios might be placed together not due to human-readable categories, but because they belong to the same category in time.

virtual architecture.definition: Models of knowledge systems overlaid with organizational structures and made accessible for public exploration, foreshadowed by Renaissance memory theaters and realized in digital spaces like cyberspace.
virtual architecture.context: Memory theater models return this recollection to the public. They wanted to render knowledge both universal and universally accessible, and they foreshadowed an idea of virtual architecture—models overlaid with knowledge systems for public access—that would be reanimated centuries later in cyberspace.

common.definition: A mode of resource production alongside capital, characterized by shared stewardship and the distribution of benefits to the largest public through peer coordination.
common.context: As Giuliani & Vercellone argue, common is a mode of resource production in the same way capital is. These modes have internal logic[s] which animate productive entities (e.g., commons, companies).
common.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

commons.definition: A local manifestation of the common mode logic where a set of peers collectively build and steward resources of mutual interest, sharing responsibility for shaping the system.
commons.context: Each commons is a local manifestation of the greater common mode logic. Here's my framing for how they produce and allocate resources.
commons.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

anti-rival.definition: A characteristic of digital goods where their social value increases as they are used more broadly, unlike material goods whose value decreases with consumption.
anti-rival.context: For many digital goods, their real (social) value . . . increases the more they are used, in stark contrast to material goods, whose value almost always decreases as they are used and consumed.
anti-rival.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

non-excludable.definition: A property of resources, particularly open source software, where external actors cannot be prevented from using, modifying, or accessing the resource.
non-excludable.context: Open Source Software (OSS) licensing enables actors external to the production process to use, modify, and suggest changes to the software. Different licenses on this software can create different levels of excludability, but the overall expectation is that others will use and modify the software, and that the code is publicly accessible.
non-excludable.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

excludability.definition: The degree to which anyone can be prevented from using a resource or consuming its benefits.
excludability.context: The standard framework for comparing the resources produced by these systems considers two main characteristics: Excludability: can anyone be prevented from using the resource?
excludability.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

rivalry.definition: The degree to which someone's use of a resource prevents another from using it, also known as subtractability; measures how much one person's consumption removes from the total available.
rivalry.context: Rivalry: does someone's use of the resource prevent another from using it? This term is also known as subtractability: to what degree someone's use removes a portion from the total available.
rivalry.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

enclosure.definition: A dynamic where external actors co-opt part or all of a commons resource output towards private benefit, restricting the benefit distribution to the involved peers.
enclosure.context: In the common mode of production, the benefits/assurances/surplus value are under the domain of involved peers. Because commons are suited for producing unmonetized and yet still valuable artifacts, other modes like capital find their way to the edges. This produces a dynamic where external actors may encroach on the peer production, or co-opt part or all of the resource output towards private benefit.
enclosure.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

egregore.definition: A non-physical entity that exists through the collective ritual activities of a group yet operates autonomously according to its own internal logic to materially influence and control the group's activities.
egregore.context: It's interesting to frame the resource and its structure as an entity, or an 'egregore.' This is a non-physical being which exists in virtue of the collective ritual activities of a group yet operates autonomously, according to its own internal logic, to materially influence and control the group's activities.
egregore.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

commons-based peer production.definition: A production model where peers collaborate to create resources of mutual interest, with the underlying process and surplus value made fully available to the entire contributor graph.
commons-based peer production.context: The underlying process, resource output, surplus value/positive externalities generated in the production are all fully available to the entire contributor graph. It's unlikely that commons resource would be stewarded in the same way or have the same characteristics outside this set of peer relationships. Yochai Benkler describes this dynamic as 'commons based peer production.'
commons-based peer production.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

boundary of the firm.definition: The shifting permeability between commons production and capital production when contributors simultaneously participate in both modes through employment relationships.
boundary of the firm.context: In both of these approaches, contributors simultaneously participate in the common and capital modes of production. Benkler describes this as 'the boundary of the firm becom[ing] more porous.'
boundary of the firm.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

benevolent dictator for life (bdfl).definition: A social/governance role recognized in open source communities where a single individual holds significant informal authority and deference on project direction, despite lacking formal override power.
benevolent dictator for life (bdfl).context: Social dynamics: contributors must cooperate to create software of this scale and complexity. Linus has been unofficially designated BDFL (benevolent dictator for life). The term recognizes the significant weight, and even deference, the community gives his opinions on the direction of Linux.
benevolent dictator for life (bdfl).source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

knowledge commons.definition: A publicly accessible, widely available, rich dataset of organizational, financial, and cultural relationships that can be verified by anyone accessing it.
knowledge commons.context: The chain data can be called a 'Knowledge Commons'—the records are available for anyone to verify: a widely available, rich dataset of organizational, financial, and cultural relationships.
knowledge commons.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

embedded capital.definition: Capital circuits and financial incentives that are directly integrated into the protocol production layer from inception, rather than being added later by independent commercial entities.
embedded capital.context: Perhaps most significantly: the Ethereum commons has capital circuits directly embedded within itself at the level of production. Monetization/productization/commodification isn't added later by an independent company (as in Linux): the software is birthed with perpetual incentives.
embedded capital.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

political polycentrism.definition: A governance norm where power and decision-making are distributed across multiple centers rather than concentrated in a single authority, promoting technical robustness through diversity.
political polycentrism.context: The diversity of client approaches is the product of and reinforces the norm of political polycentrism. In an ideal case, there is a healthy distribution of many client types. This produces a more technically robust, fault-tolerant network.
political polycentrism.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

network-bound state.definition: A shared state or history that is distributed across a global network where all actors must come to consensus on a single instantiation, creating enhanced anti-rival characteristics.
network-bound state.context: They might share the same blockspace/state/history: network-bound state. This enhances the anti-rival characteristics of the resource.
network-bound state.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

protocol surface area.definition: The accessible interfaces and decomposable components of a protocol that allow external actors to build adjacent systems without requiring centralized control.
protocol surface area.context: Relative to Linux, the EVM ecosystem is a public system that lends itself to decomposition of the blockspace production stack, aka 'protocol surface area.' This makes it harder for any single capital entity/small group to dominate (absent cartelization) over longer timelines.
protocol surface area.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

usable right away.definition: A characteristic of software artifacts that produce value immediately upon deployment without requiring additional external work to create a complete product.
usable right away.context: Whereas the Linux kernel doesn't produce anything for users until distros add their features, running Ethereum software produces a usable artifact right away. From the genesis block, Ethereum has always had a broad range of individual enthusiasts, communities, organizations, and infrastructure all using the chain at the same time.
usable right away.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

single global artifact.definition: A software system that produces a single, unified, publicly distributed instantiation of state and history across all participating nodes rather than isolated instances.
single global artifact.context: Operators from around the world run the client software releases and come to consensus on a single instantiation of state and history (i.e., 'mainnet' 'chainID=1' 'ETH L1'). In contrast to Linux (the kernel doesn't produce anything on its own, distros needed to produce many isolated/private instances), the Ethereum software commons outputs a single, public software artifact.
single global artifact.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

acquihire.definition: A practice where capital entities acquire a team building a project primarily to gain access to the team's technical skills, knowledge, and political/social relationships within the ecosystem.
acquihire.context: A large multinational corporation has projects adjacent to but outside of the commons. They acquihire the team building a Layer 2, which gives them access to the political/social relationships which comprise the Ethereum software commons.
acquihire.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

crowding out.definition: A phenomenon where extrinsic motivations (financial incentives) displace intrinsic motivations (passion, peer respect, intellectual challenge) in driving commons stewardship.
crowding out.context: Commons stewardship that leans too heavily on the presence of capital (extrinsic motivations) risks crowding out intrinsic motivations (e.g., vibes, respect from peers, challenging oneself).
crowding out.source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

maximal extractable value (mev).definition: The maximum value that can be extracted from block production in excess of the standard block reward and gas fees by including, excluding, and changing the order of transactions in a block.
maximal extractable value (mev).context: Blockspace (and any associated MEV) can be considered a separate infrastructure/resource supply chain. Maximal extractable value (MEV) refers to the maximum value that can be extracted from block production in excess of the standard block reward and gas fees by including, excluding, and changing the order of transactions in a block.
maximal extractable value (mev).source: Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux and Ethereum

social protocols.definition: Codified procedures that coordinate human behavior through device-mediated systems, excluding individual habits and rituals.
social protocols.context: Social protocols are codified procedures that coordinate human behavior; the habits and rituals of an individual are excluded. Timekeeping is a device-mediated social protocol—various forms of timekeeping, supported by different tools, dictate how one may mark or tell time.

device-mediated social protocol.definition: A coordinated behavioral system implemented through specific material tools or devices that structure how groups interact with a shared practice.
device-mediated social protocol.context: Timekeeping is a device-mediated social protocol—various forms of timekeeping, supported by different tools, dictate how one may mark or tell time.

good protocols.definition: Protocols that constrain human behavior in order to liberate or enable participants, where the majority subjectively experience them as worth following in net liberty.
good protocols.context: Good protocols constrain in order to liberate or enable. Whether a protocol leads to an overall sense of liberation or enablement must be subjectively defined: if most who participate in the protocol feel that it is worth it in net liberty, we could say that this protocol has achieved the status of good.

horological politics.definition: The study of how timekeeping devices and systems are used as instruments of political control, social order, and power assertion.
horological politics.context: The visible imposition of time has very often been a deliberate means of exerting control over lives. Sometimes, this display of control is meant to achieve a sense of security through projecting order in chaotic times.

protocol consciousness.definition: The shift in awareness and understanding that occurs as people internalize and integrate a protocol into society, changing their mental frameworks and values.
protocol consciousness.context: As it becomes more internalized and integrated into society, the protocol changes the consciousness of people. There is no ground-truth sentiment to measure goodness by.

discrete interval time.definition: A timekeeping experience where time is presented as individual, separate units or moments marked by distinct signals.
discrete interval time.context: Some devices dole out time as discrete intervals, such as metronomes, quartz watches with ticking second hands, or the British cannon in Cape Town that fires at noon.

continuous time experience.definition: A timekeeping phenomenology where time is experienced as flowing smoothly rather than in distinct intervals, bringing temporal continuity into consciousness.
continuous time experience.context: Other devices create a more continuous experience of time—hourglasses, candle clocks, or wristwatches with sweeping second hands. The sweeping second hand or the sinking candle wax may pass through regularly-spaced interval markers, but they are more able to bring the continuity of each interval into one's consciousness.

device consciousness.definition: The relationship between the material properties of timekeeping instruments and how they shape human awareness and experience of time itself.
device consciousness.context: The ways in which we protocolize marking and telling time are intertwined with clocks, calendars, and the other devices that shape and are shaped by the protocols.

incense clock.definition: An intricate timekeeping device originating in medieval China that uses maze-like patterns of burning incense to mark time intervals through scent and visual progression.
incense clock.context: The more intricate incense clock originated in China in the Song Dynasty. One stencils powdered incense into a maze-like structure and lights the end; the various twists and turns in the maze mark intervals of hours.

yin hours and yang hours.definition: In Chinese incense clock design, even-numbered hours designated as yin (passive, introverted) and odd-numbered hours as yang (active, extroverted), with activities matched to hour type.
yin hours and yang hours.context: There were twelve hours in a day; even-numbered hours were yin—which were considered more passive, introverted hours—and odd-numbered hours were yang—more active, extroverted hours. Activities recommended for yin hours included introspection, meditation, and rest.

temporal order.definition: The imposition of systematic, regulated timekeeping on a population to instill a sense of civic order and exercise social control.
temporal order.context: By instilling temporal order, public clock towers also aim to instill a sense of civic order. This civic order can generate a sense of comfort—or not, depending on which people are controlling time for which people's attention.

temperance (as moral virtue of time).definition: A civic and religious virtue elevated in medieval Christian culture to represent disciplined, careful management of one's temporal allocations and actions.
temperance (as moral virtue of time).context: Around the same time, time and timekeeping became equated religiously with temperance, the civic virtue elevated beyond the others: fortitude, justice, prudence, and magnanimity were subsumed to temperance, which was even compared to Christ.

clock-time versus natural time.definition: The distinction between abstract, mathematically regulated temporal measurement (clock-time) and time as experienced through natural phenomena and rhythms.
clock-time versus natural time.context: Clock-time makes natural time unconscious, not in a way where we follow it more readily, but in a way where we barely follow it at all. At some point in Western history, clock time became more regular than, and increasingly separated from, the rhythms of nature.

knotted cord (time alarm).definition: An accessible timekeeping device used by sentries made from punk wood knotted at intervals and ignited, with burning down to the skin serving as a wake signal.
knotted cord (time alarm).context: The knotted cord was commonly used as a time alarm amongst the poorest Chinese. This was a cord made from punk—dry decayed wood—knotted at intervals. A military sentry on night duty would wedge the punk cord between his bare toes, with the correct knot-lengths sticking out, and ignite it at the start of the watch.

phenomenology of time.definition: The lived, subjective experience and conscious awareness of temporal passage shaped by specific timekeeping devices and methods.
phenomenology of time.context: Phenomenologically, a cannon is experienced very differently from a clock tower: associated with war and death, the boom of a cannon carries for miles. Symbolically, it conveys a different message from a local timepiece for a city's citizens.

time distribution.definition: The process by which timekeeping information is disseminated across a population, requiring infrastructure and social coordination beyond mere timekeeping itself.
time distribution.context: The noon-day gun in Cape Town had real utility for this reason; pocket watches were scarce and inaccurate and required their wearers to remember to wind them—ultimately, people did come to rely on the daily blast. Time is not only kept; to be widely followed, it must also be distributed.

horological supremacy.definition: The technological and political dominance achieved through mastery of clockwork manufacturing, used to justify and assert imperial control.
horological supremacy.context: The British's horological supremacy at the height of the empire—London was the center of the clock industry—helped them both to justify (via a sense of technological superiority) and to assert their colonial dominance.

materiality of timekeeping infrastructur.definition: The physical and material properties of timekeeping devices that determine what aspects of time become conscious or unconscious in a population's experience.
materiality of timekeeping infrastructur.context: The materiality of timekeeping infrastructure determines what and how the protocol is carried out, and what is brought to the fore of one's consciousness and what is overlooked.

sands of time.definition: A metaphor derived from hourglasses that represents the inevitable passage and finitude of human life, emphasizing impermanence.
sands of time.context: As a unique enduring symbol of impermanence and finitude, the 'sands of time' is a metaphor for the shortness of human life. Hourglasses have been depicted on pirate flags (to menace viewers) and on gravestones, and placed in English coffins.

protocolization of timekeeping.definition: The process by which timekeeping methods become codified into explicit, enforceable social protocols that structure collective behavior.
protocolization of timekeeping.context: The ways in which we protocolize marking and telling time are intertwined with clocks, calendars, and the other devices that shape and are shaped by the protocols.

liberatory constraints.definition: Protocol restrictions that, while limiting certain freedoms, enable and liberate participants by reducing unnecessary decision-making and providing predictable structure for action.
liberatory constraints.context: Good protocols liberate in the same way disciplined habits and routines can liberate artists. If we succeed at evolving a protocol with the right liberatory constraints in the right places, the risk we take is that—being never quite moored to anything more stable—it changes us somehow, once again.

atomized time measurement.definition: The modern practice of measuring time through the imperceptible regularities of atomic oscillation rather than observable natural phenomena.
atomized time measurement.context: Instead mooring our time to the imperceptible regularities of the atom. We direct our prized technological sophistication towards keeping out the elements—temperature fluctuations, humidity, quantum gravity effects—from our expensive atomic clocks so that we can track homogenous, perfectly regular intervals ever-better.

exploration-exploitation tradeoff.definition: The strategic balance between trying new options (exploration) that may lead to better outcomes and choosing the best-known option (exploitation); finding the optimal balance is crucial in decision-making situations aiming to maximize long-term benefits.
exploration-exploitation tradeoff.context: When playing a game (or making any decision), a player has to make a decision between the two strategies of exploration and exploitation... The ideal strategy for many singles is to date around enough to find someone worthy of marrying, the 'game' is of a finite length.

geosocial dating.definition: A form of dating enabled by mobile phones that helps people find potential partners based on geographic proximity using location-sharing technology, with profiles largely based on images.
geosocial dating.context: Since mobile phones enable location sharing, apps like the gay-male-focused Grindr were built to help people find potential sexual partners based on geographic proximity in a new form of dating known as geosocial dating.

dating pipeline.definition: A funnel-like process borrowed from sales methodology where individuals source, qualify, and progress potential dates through stages (kissing/hooking up, seeing one another, becoming a couple, engagement, marriage) or reject them, treating dating analogous to a sales process.
dating pipeline.context: In the same way that a sales rep sources leads, qualifies them, and then closes deals, people use apps to source dates. These dates either progress to later stages in the pipeline (kissing/hooking up, formally seeing one another, becoming a couple, and eventually, perhaps, getting engaged, then married) or eventually fail to.

flow market.definition: A market where successful navigation means exiting the market entirely; in dating, successfully finding a relationship means no longer needing to look for one, though people may re-enter and re-exit in the future.
flow market.context: Dating, on the other hand, is a flow market. Successfully navigating the market means exiting the market, i.e., successfully finding a relationship and no longer needing to look for one.

protocol consensus.definition: A sufficient critical mass of people at scale who are aware of and engaged with a protocol for that protocol to function effectively.
protocol consensus.context: As we'll see later, attempts to subvert swipe-based protocols all suffer from insufficient market liquidity. This is crucial as some degree of 'protocol consensus' is necessary for dating protocols to work at all—enough people need to be aware of and bought into a protocol for the protocol to work.

principal-agent problem.definition: A conflict in interests and priorities that arises when one entity (the agent) takes actions on behalf of another entity (the principal), creating misaligned incentives.
principal-agent problem.context: This is a standard principal-agent problem: conflict in interests and priorities that arises when one person or entity (the agent) takes actions on behalf of another person or entity (the principal).

flattening.definition: The process of reducing one's dynamic, multifaceted identity to fit the constraints of a digital platform's design, sacrificing authenticity and uniqueness to maximize algorithmic compatibility.
flattening.context: Dating protocol participants are incentivized to protocolize their own identities to better participate in the protocol. This is a type of flattening—sacrificing your dynamic identity in order to fit with the 'flat' nature of digital dating apps, as currently conceived.

ghosting.definition: The act of abruptly ceasing all communication and contact with a dating match without explanation, leaving the other person without closure.
ghosting.context: Most matches fail. That's because many of them don't lead to conversation. And the ones that do start a conversation have a high rate of ghosting.

dangerous protocols.definition: Protocols that are neither inherently good nor bad but operate in ways that control participants completely, demand loyalty in relinquishing decision-making power, and lack central mediation making escape difficult.
dangerous protocols.context: In an essay, Nadia Asparouhova introduces the idea that protocols are neither good, nor bad, but dangerous. She argues that protocols 'do not liberate us, but rather control us completely'.

stable yet suboptimal protocol.definition: A protocol that functions adequately and maintains relative equilibrium but leaves participants feeling unsatisfied and unfulfilled despite technical stability.
stable yet suboptimal protocol.context: Being trapped in protocols dictated by a functional-yet-suboptimal system feels eerily calm, yet unsatisfying. Everything works, sort of, but participants feel a curious lack of fulfillment.

swiping.definition: A dating app mechanic where users see one profile at a time and make a binary decision to swipe left (reject) or right (accept), with matches only occurring when both users swipe right on each other.
swiping.context: Tinder later adopted these same features but also introduced the notion of swiping—showing users only one profile at a time until a user decisively swiped left (rejected) or right (accepted).

mimetic spreading.definition: The process by which successful dating profile strategies or messages spread across the ecosystem through imitation, leading to homogenization and loss of individuality in how users present themselves.
mimetic spreading.context: Even when an opening message or dating profile bio is successful at driving engagement yet nonspecific enough to attract a broad net of leads, it mimetically spreads across the ecosystem. Suddenly you have tons of men who've written the same 'Looking for the Pam to my Jim,' profile title.

arranged marriage protocol.definition: A historic dating and partnership protocol where parents and elders assess compatibility based on shared religion, culture, and values rather than romantic choice, emphasizing practical expectations over physical attractiveness and romantic ideals.
arranged marriage protocol.context: Arranged marriages have been the historic 'protocol of choice' for South Asian, Middle Eastern, African, Jewish (primarily Ashkenazi and Sephardic), and other communities. Each of these cultures emphasizes the importance of family in decision making.

overfitting.definition: In dating context, having so many specific criteria for a potential partner that one filters out effectively all candidates, making it impossible to create a pipeline of leads to explore or exploit.
overfitting.context: Tradwife seekers often fail to find a suitable partner because of overfitting: having so many criteria they filter for that they source effectively no leads at all.

tradwife.definition: A woman who adopts traditional sex roles and expectations within marriage, typically rejecting contemporary models of equal partnership in favor of anachronistic gender norms and domestic roles.
tradwife.context: A tradwife (a neologism for traditional wife or traditional housewife), in recent Western culture, typically denotes a woman who believes in traditional sex roles and a traditional marriage.

pareto principle (in dating).definition: The 80/20 rule applied to dating markets, whereby approximately 80% of women compete for the top 20% of men, creating a lopsided distribution of attention and matching success.
pareto principle (in dating).context: The Pareto principle (80/20 rule) states that 80% of the consequences come from 20% of causes. And it applies to dating: the top (i.e., most attractive) ~80% of women on dating apps compete for the top ~20% of men.

match conversion.definition: The process by which a match on a dating app progresses to an actual in-person meeting or meaningful interaction, as opposed to remaining a virtual connection that never materializes.
match conversion.context: Despite the success of dating apps in creating matches, whether the matches made on these apps are meaningful or conducive to long-term pair-bonding, is actively debated. Most Bumble matches continue to fail to 'convert.'

sexual validation.definition: The psychological satisfaction and confidence boost derived from being desired or matched by others on dating apps, separate from the instrumental goal of actually dating or meeting someone.
sexual validation.context: Seeing who also swipes right on you satisfies curiosity and a basic human need for sexual validation... A match feels like a confidence-boost; it is a sign that the Other sees you and likes you.

bioregion.definition: A geographic area defined by ecological characteristics such as soil composition, climate patterns, and unique flora and fauna distribution, rather than political boundaries.
bioregion.context: The bioregion contains 75 ecoregions. Common to all the cities within it are not country or state, but rather soil composition, climate patterns, and unique flora and fauna distributions.
bioregion.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

global protocol network.definition: An open-membership, shared policy system of approximately 7,462 cities worldwide that coordinates governance through adaptable, place-based protocols while maintaining local decision-making autonomy.
global protocol network.context: the city today stands as a testament to the transformation created by 7,462 cities around the world that together form the Global Protocol Network: an open-membership, shared policy system built with the flexibility and ongoing adaptability of local governance in mind.

bio-regional protocol.definition: A foundational governance protocol that replaces absolute political borders with permeable, overlapping boundaries based on actual resource constraints and ecological zones.
bio-regional protocol.context: By doing away with absolute borders in favor of permeable, overlapping ones based on actual resource constraints, the protocol created a new kind of political common ground. But this time through place, instead of in spite of it.
bio-regional protocol.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

core protocol.definition: A globally-adopted protocol framework that provides foundational policy structure and scaffolding while allowing local jurisdictions to implement and modify it according to their specific contexts and needs.
core protocol.context: Core FSP functions as a half-built house. Provided with a global barebones framework, each jurisdiction makes its own local copy, makes some tweaks, and then goes about filling it in and decorating to meet their community's tastes and needs.

sub-protocol.definition: A specialized governance component nested within a core protocol that addresses a specific function or domain while inheriting the core protocol's general structure and policies.
sub-protocol.context: one such core policy, known as a sub-protocol, is the Urban Rewilding Protocol (URP). URP oversees the need to set aside a certain fraction of urban land specifically for native plants and pollinators.

coastal disaster protocol.definition: A protocol for managing coastal hazards through nature-based solutions like seaweed cultivation and blue-green infrastructure to attenuate waves, build natural shorelines, and restore sustainable mariculture.
coastal disaster protocol.context: their approach to saltwater intrusion and Coastal Disaster Protocol (CDP), which involves a triple bottom-line approach involving nature-based solutions. More specifically it is a protocol for managing coastal disaster events, with a first approach leveraging blue-green infrastructure, such as seaweed farms and clam gardens.

forest stewardship protocol.definition: A protocol that guides the long-term management and restoration of forests through Indigenous knowledge and community stewardship to maintain biodiversity and resource productivity.
forest stewardship protocol.context: It wasn't until Indigenous communities came in as collaborators and were later funded through a process that gave them full control of long-term fund allocation and distribution, that it was discovered these biodiversity hotspots were a result of human hands and have since been re-adopted as an industry standard.
forest stewardship protocol.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

food systems protocol.definition: A core governance protocol that establishes a distributed urban agricultural system with specific land allocation percentages for food production, native plants, and community control over local food growing and distribution.
food systems protocol.context: Core FSP functions as a half-built house. Provided with a global barebones framework, each jurisdiction makes its own local copy, makes some tweaks, and then goes about filling it in and decorating to meet their community's tastes and needs.
food systems protocol.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

urban rewilding protocol.definition: A sub-protocol that establishes guidelines and ratios for dedicating urban land to native plants and pollinators, supporting natural pest control, pollination, and soil restoration while allowing local jurisdictions to set specific implementation details.
urban rewilding protocol.context: one such core policy, known as a sub-protocol, is the Urban Rewilding Protocol (URP). URP oversees the need to set aside a certain fraction of urban land specifically for native plants and pollinators.

half-built house.definition: A metaphor for core protocols that provide foundational scaffolding and barebones frameworks while expecting local jurisdictions to fill in and customize implementation details according to their specific needs.
half-built house.context: Core FSP functions as a half-built house. Provided with a global barebones framework, each jurisdiction makes its own local copy, makes some tweaks, and then goes about filling it in and decorating to meet their community's tastes and needs.

downward merge.definition: The process by which changes made to a local protocol implementation can be pushed upward to the core protocol level for consideration by the wider network.
downward merge.context: Similarly, if a local implementation makes any core changes, they have the option to push the changes up to the core level. While these downward merges and upward pushes aren't always accepted by every city in the network or integrated into the core protocol, they are still accessible to any jurisdiction.

upward push.definition: A process where local implementations of a protocol can propose changes that potentially get integrated into the core protocol level if approved.
upward push.context: Similarly, if a local implementation makes any core changes, they have the option to push the changes up to the core level. While these downward merges and upward pushes aren't always accepted by every city in the network or integrated into the core protocol, they are still accessible to any jurisdiction.
upward push.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

global protocol marketplace.definition: A platform where open-source apps, tools, and protocol implementations are shared, copied, modified, and deployed by any city or jurisdiction within or outside the Global Protocol Network.
global protocol marketplace.context: available for any city within and outside the network to adopt and modify as part of their own set of governing protocols or general governance through a platform known as the Global Protocol Marketplace.

base produce.definition: Essential food items grown by every neighborhood or outsourced to nearby rural farms to meet the city's basic nutritional needs and ensure food security.
base produce.context: Base produce is food that's grown by every neighborhood and/or outsourced to nearby rural farms to meet the city's basic needs.
base produce.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

specific produce.definition: A growing list of foods unique to each neighborhood that residents choose to cultivate for themselves, with a percentage allocated to farmers markets for local sharing.
specific produce.context: Specific produce, on the other hand, is a growing list unique to every neighborhood and contains plants they will grow specifically for themselves, and allocate a percentage of to the farmer's markets.

rhizomatic scaling.definition: A horizontal expansion strategy where governance or systems grow by duplicating and distributing across many small nodes rather than centralizing through a single authority, drawing from botanical metaphor of rhizome root systems.
rhizomatic scaling.context: Otieno says their goal was to scale horizontally, staying small and duplicating as they expanded, and to have no central authority... they needed this to grow rhizomatically if it was going to scale to the level it needed to.

interoperability.definition: The capacity of protocol apps and policy components to seamlessly share users, data, and functionality across different implementations and jurisdictions.
interoperability.context: The key is that each app is composable and interoperable, meaning they are able to share users and data, and can be copied and run anywhere, by anyone.

supermodularity.definition: A technical architecture principle where core load-bearing components are designed to restrict failures to subcomponents rather than causing cascading system failures across the entire protocol.
supermodularity.context: The technical term for this design is called supermodularity, which Das says restricts most failures or issues to subcomponents, rather than turning into cascading failure events.

produce inventory protocol.definition: A sub-protocol that uses sales and consumption data to determine which foods need to be grown or processed annually and categorizes them into Base produce and Specific produce for distribution.
produce inventory protocol.context: Another sub-protocol core to the FSP is the Produce Inventory Protocol which uses produce and general sales data to determine which foods people are buying and how much needs to be grown or processed every year to meet demand.

community-actualization.definition: A continuous process where individuals pursue self-realization while simultaneously contributing to the collective wellbeing and development of their community.
community-actualization.context: regardless, I realised that safe now wasn't always going to be safe in the future, and through my new work self-actualization quickly turned into a continuous process of community-actualization.

protocol currency.definition: A specialized medium of exchange assigned to each protocol that tracks the specific kinds of value it enables and makes visible the flow of work, resources, and ecological health through a region.
protocol currency.context: Hui put forth a proposal for each protocol to be assigned its own currency to keep track of the specific kind of value it enables and how it moves through a region.

value flow.definition: The movement and transaction of protocol-specific currencies through a city, making visible the exchange of resources, labor, and ecological health.
value flow.context: Instead, different currencies are employed to track and measure each of these unique forms of value and make their flow paths more visible and transparent as they flow through the city in the form of transactions.
value flow.source: Features from the Future: Dispatches from Cascadia

expired rules.definition: Regulations and bylaws that no longer serve current community needs and have become obstacles to adaptive governance and local problem-solving.
expired rules.context: If a city councillor or the police force didn't like what we were doing with the urban farms or wanted to fine us for violating any existing rules, I called them 'expired rules' since they no longer served our needs.

flywheel economy.definition: An economic system where incremental improvements and restoration efforts create positive feedback loops that accelerate growth and enable larger subsequent initiatives.
flywheel economy.context: what they were actually doing was restoring soils and biodiversity, while also creating a flywheel-like economy for rewilding. Without those years of restored land and increased native pollinator species, we never would have been able to build the urban farm network as fast as we did.

bioregional protocol.definition: A governance framework that organizes political jurisdictions around ecological boundaries like watersheds and ecoregions rather than traditional political borders, enabling resource management aligned with natural constraints.
bioregional protocol.context: The Bio-Regional Protocol was officially acknowledged by cities that were part of the North and South American Continental Network in 2032, and was later activated at the Global Network level in 2035, after we iterated a bit more on its design.

value flow blockage.definition: A disruption in the circulation of protocol currency indicating contamination or degradation in a system that requires remediation before normal value flow can resume.
value flow blockage.context: If a river is contaminated, its currency value decreases and the flow may be stopped until it's safe again. When this happens, it's a sign to us that there's a value flow blockage that needs to be addressed properly.

data-sharing agreement.definition: Formal arrangements between cities or jurisdictions specifying what categories of data are shared, at what scale, and under what governance conditions to enable collective sensing and coordinated resource distribution.
data-sharing agreement.context: central to protocolized governance is a data-sharing agreement that between and within cities. It's a way for the cities in the Global Protocol Network to sense each other and their needs without always having to explicitly ask for help.

universal id.definition: A globally recognized identifier that enables individuals to maintain a single, consistent identity across multiple organizations, platforms, and networks.
universal id.context: Unlike other leading software, Flow is built on the rich world of Open Protocols: Use your Universal ID, sync your Assistant, and integrate your Personal Intellectual Property licensing contracts.

collective intelligence.definition: The combined knowledge, resources, and problem-solving capabilities that emerge when a team works in synchronized coordination and shared context.
collective intelligence.context: With Flow, not only will you be able to manage your tasks and communication more effectively, but you will also tap into a new dimension of Collective Intelligence.

algorithmic preference private id.definition: A personalized identifier that captures an individual's information path blueprint and learning history, allowing systems to accelerate personalization by accessing what other machine systems have already learned about that person.
algorithmic preference private id.context: Flow takes personalization to the next level by uploading your Algorithmic Preference Private ID, which you may know as your information path blueprint. This allows Flow to access what other machine systems have already learned about you, dramatically accelerating the personalization process.

signal calibration.definition: The process of filtering and routing information so that the right data reaches the right people at the right time, reducing noise and cognitive overload.
signal calibration.context: Signal Calibration and Focus Control. Our customizable algorithms ensure that the right information reaches the right people at the right time, adapting to your business needs and personal preferences.

public registry of certified information.definition: A continuously updated, globally accessible knowledge base of verified documents, discussions, and expertise that extends beyond organizational boundaries.
public registry of certified information.context: Flow allows you to communicate with anyone online and search the Public Registry of Certified Information. Imagine having a curated set of journal articles and advice from your mentor in every conversation.

attunement.definition: The continuous process of aligning team members' tasks, skills, availability, and emotional context to ensure synchronized collaboration toward shared objectives.
