attunement.context: Flow continuously adjusts tasks across your team based on skills, priorities, availability, and emotional context. When enabled, Flow automatically and continuously reforms roles based on employee preferences and opportunities.

neurostate.definition: A module that uses science-backed insights to help individuals sustainably manage mental well-being and productivity while rebalancing workload across teams to prevent burnout.
neurostate.context: NeuroState empowers you to sustainably manage your mental well-being and productivity. Flow equips you with personalized, science-backed recommendations to help you preempt stress and burnout.

sonarscape analytics.definition: A feature that translates business processes and organizational data into dynamic soundscapes, providing an intuitive auditory way to understand and respond to a company's operational pulse.
sonarscape analytics.context: Turn data into dynamic soundscapes with SonarScape. Our groundbreaking Flow feature translates your business processes into music, offering a novel, intuitive way to understand and feel your company's pulse, energizing your team like never before.

talismanic tools.definition: Digital rituals and features designed to deepen team unity, foster meaningful connections, and align members with organizational goals through symbolic and ceremonial practices.
talismanic tools.context: These aren't just 'features,' they're digital rituals designed to deepen team unity, foster meaningful connections, and keep everyone aligned with the larger organizational goals. From setting collective visions to celebrating achievements, Flow's Talismanic Tools foster team bonding and supports your shared mission.

team sentiment awareness.definition: The capability to monitor and understand the emotional and psychological state of team members to inform coordination and task allocation decisions.
team sentiment awareness.context: TeamSentiment Awareness. Proactively Reduces Risk of TeamBurnout.

teamserendipity engine.definition: A feature that proactively surfaces unexpected connections, resources, and collaborators that benefit team members at opportune moments.
teamserendipity engine.context: TeamSerendipity Engine. People just seem to get unstuck, coming across new resources right when they need them.

sight.definition: A personalized content horizon that allows users to narrow or broaden their visibility of organizational information, from laser focus on urgent tasks to expansive team activity awareness.
sight.context: Say, 'Adjust my Sight,' to narrow or broaden your content horizon. Whether you want laser focus on urgent tasks or an expansive view of team activities, Sight keeps you in sync and in tune with your team.

contextually aware environment.definition: A system that synthesizes messages, documents, and insights and delivers them based on understanding the user's current task, needs, and organizational context.
contextually aware environment.context: Flow introduces you to a contextually aware, Seamless, Intelligent, and Adaptive environment. Each message, task, document, and insight is first synthesized together and then delivered to you and your team.

open protocols.definition: Standardized, interoperable frameworks that enable communication and data exchange across different systems, organizations, and platforms without vendor lock-in.
open protocols.context: Unlike other leading software, Flow is built on the rich world of Open Protocols: Use your Universal ID, sync your Assistant, and integrate your Personal Intellectual Property licensing contracts.

permissive ip.definition: An intellectual property framework that allows individuals to integrate their innovations, patents, and proprietary knowledge into collaborative systems while maintaining security and attribution.
permissive ip.context: To complete the setup, say, 'Sync my IP.' This will integrate your existing Permissive IP into Flow, integrate your licensing agreements, and ensure your innovations are credited and protected within the Flow environment.

algorithmic symphony.definition: The integration of an individual's algorithmic preferences across multiple systems so that personalization is harmonized and consistent across all platforms.
algorithmic symphony.context: Flow integrates your algorithmic preferences so your work and team are in harmony with your mind. By connecting other systems, you are not starting from scratch; you're standing on the shoulders of your own digital history, making Flow attune to you, not the other way around.

groupthink.definition: A rare system malfunction (~1:10^5) where team members experience cognitive alignment influenced by external factors or dominant personalities, reducing independent thought and healthy conflict.
groupthink.context: While rare (~1:10^5), team members may experience 'groupthink,' influenced by external factors or individual personalities within the team. To mitigate this, we recommend the following: (1) Diversify your data inputs to prevent a homogeneous flow of information across team members.

ghosts.definition: Phantom profiles or tasks generated by Flow for non-existent personnel, a rare system artifact (~1:10^7) that requires synchronization with current network records.
ghosts.context: In rare instances (~1:10^7), Flow may generate profiles or tasks for non-existent personnel, commonly referred to as 'ghosts' or 'phantoms'. Regularly synchronize Flow with your Network Contract Information System for up-to-date people and autonomous agent records.

continuous team role realignment.definition: An automated process that dynamically reassigns roles and responsibilities across team members based on evolving skills, preferences, availability, and organizational needs.
continuous team role realignment.context: Continuous Team Role Realignment. Flow automatically and continuously reforms roles based on employee preferences and opportunities.

universal intelligence standards.definition: Global technical standards that enable Flow to work seamlessly with all standard voice commands, hand gestures, eye movements, and machine-aid languages.
universal intelligence standards.context: Flow leverages today's Universal Intelligence Standards (UIS). That means that Flow works with all standard voice commands, hand gestures, and eye movements. Flow supports all human languages, as well as machine-aid shorthands such as BOT_VERSE and UNI_PROMPT.

for-you-profile.definition: A personalized dashboard that synthesizes an individual's daily milestones, meeting contexts, and personalized insights upon login.
for-you-profile.context: The 'For-You-Profile' is ready as soon as you log in. Just say, 'Good morning, Flow,' to get a rundown of your day's milestones, meeting contexts, and personalized insights.

zero-knowledge privacy preserving standa.definition: Data management protocols that enable Flow to collect and analyze user information while protecting individual privacy and preventing access to raw personal data.
zero-knowledge privacy preserving standa.context: By using the Flow platform, you agree to the management of such data via zero-knowledge privacy preserving standards for the purposes outlined in our Privacy Policy.

fire protocols.definition: Explicit coordination systems and practices that enable communities to work with fire as an essential tool and way of life rather than a destructive force to be suppressed.
fire protocols.context: Fire protocols seek to adapt communities to fire as an essential tool and way of life rather than a destructive force to be suppressed at all costs.
fire protocols.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

fire-ecology to fire-climate transition.definition: The historical shift in California from an ecosystem naturally shaped by fire cycles to one where atmospheric heating has fundamentally altered fire behavior and management possibilities.
fire-ecology to fire-climate transition.context: After a century of fire suppression and heating atmospheric conditions, California has changed from a fire-ecology to a fire-climate; our ability to work with fire is reshaping how we come to know the world.
fire-ecology to fire-climate transition.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

fire return interval.definition: The cyclical timeframe and ongoing relationship between prescribed fire events, understood as necessary context for sustainable fire management rather than isolated interventions.
fire return interval.context: Prescribed fire is insufficient as a stand-alone event. It must be understood within a 'fire return interval' and ongoing relationship.
fire return interval.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

attention as autopoietic space.definition: A framework where attentional practices create self-generating conditions for sensing and navigating environmental complexity, dissolving boundaries between natural and artificial knowledge systems.
attention as autopoietic space.context: Through attention, we cultivate ways of sensing and navigating the complexity of contexts.
attention as autopoietic space.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

prescribed fire practitioner.definition: A land management professional who implements controlled burns as ecological restoration; the paper argues they require a distinct identity outside of firefighting culture to sustain the practice.
prescribed fire practitioner.context: Prescribed fire practitioners require an identity outside of firefighting in order to generate a sustainable cultural shift.
prescribed fire practitioner.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

fire as public digital spectacle.definition: The contemporary phenomenon where fire events are mediated through digital technologies and apps, reshaping public interactions with transparency, identity, and crisis coordination.
fire as public digital spectacle.context: Fire is now a public digital spectacle via technologies and apps like WatchDuty and ALERT california, reshaping our interactions with transparency, identity, and coordination in crisis.
fire as public digital spectacle.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

fire affects logbook.definition: A physical archive and observational tool that helps fire practitioners cultivate attention to place and deepen their relationship with different forms of memory.
fire affects logbook.context: The Fire Affects Logbook serves as a physical archive, helping fire practitioners cultivate attention to place while deepening their personal relationship with different forms of memory.
fire affects logbook.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

kashia pomo fire protocols.definition: Indigenous fire management knowledge and practices of the Kashia Pomo people, integrated into contemporary coordination systems for prescribed burn management.
kashia pomo fire protocols.context: Integration of Kashia Pomo fire protocols into GFA coordination system.
kashia pomo fire protocols.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

subcanopy reduction.definition: The ecological process of removing understory vegetation through prescribed fire, reframed as restoration that differentiates generational growth rather than destruction.
subcanopy reduction.context: Perceiving subcanopy reduction as restoration offers a shift in how we relate to loss, seeing it not as destruction but as a necessary part of ecological renewal.
subcanopy reduction.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

geopolitical top-down structures vs. cul.term: geopolitical top-down structures vs. cultural knowledge systems
geopolitical top-down structures vs. cul.definition: The central tension between hierarchical state-mandated fire management policies and locally-rooted, culturally-embedded fire knowledge systems.
geopolitical top-down structures vs. cul.context: Geopolitical top-down structures vs. Cultural knowledge systems
geopolitical top-down structures vs. cul.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

protocol improvement.definition: A methodological approach to iteratively refining coordination systems through practical implementation, learning, and integration of diverse stakeholder knowledge.
protocol improvement.context: Protocol improvement seeks to adapt communities to fire as an essential tool through systematic testing and refinement of coordination practices.
protocol improvement.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

living memory across media and agents.term: living memory across media and agents
living memory across media and agents.definition: The capacity of knowledge and remembrance to move fluidly between different physical and social carriers—humans, objects, systems—dissolving boundaries between artificial and natural knowledge transmission.
living memory across media and agents.context: Just as living memory can move between mediums and agents, dissolving the boundaries between the artificial and the natural, so too can our relationship to weather.
living memory across media and agents.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

collective discernment.definition: The shared capacity of communities to make wise decisions while maintaining flexibility and improvisation in rapidly changing conditions.
collective discernment.context: We need practices that keep us nimble and flexible within rapidly-changing conditions, and ultimately grow our ability to improvise while maintaining collective discernment.
collective discernment.source: Fire Protocols: Attention as Autopoietic Space

protocological death.definition: The end of life for a collective entity or protocol system, which can occur through various mechanisms and requires ritual, memorial, and archival practices.
protocological death.context: The Order for Protocological Death was founded in 2038 as an independent body to oversee and administer end of life rites for collective entities called worlds.
protocological death.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

world.definition: An ecosystem of avatars and participants grown through their time and attention, characterized by borders, laws, values, and evidence of itself in members, symbols, artifacts, and media.
world.context: A world is an ecosystem of avatars, grown through their time and attention. Not every protocol can die because not every protocol lived, as a world, in the first place.

ritual deletion.definition: The ceremonial process of removing and compressing records of a protocol or world as part of end-of-life practices.
ritual deletion.context: One of the core practices of our organization is ritual deletion, leading to ever-more compressed mnemonic memorials.
ritual deletion.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by success.definition: A mode of protocol failure where the protocol becomes so successful that it outscales its initial design parameters or the rate at which it can change.
death by success.context: Death by success: when the protocol becomes so successful, it outscales its initial design parameters or possible rate of change
death by success.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by ossification.definition: A mode of protocol failure where governance processes become too rigid to allow necessary changes as the world around the protocol evolves.
death by ossification.context: Death by ossification: when the governance process becomes too rigid to allow for needed change, when the world changes and the protocol cannot
death by ossification.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by mismanagement.definition: A mode of protocol failure caused by a sufficiently poor decision made by decision-makers, independent of whether the governance process itself is functional or the protocol is healthy.
death by mismanagement.context: Death by mismanagement: when the protocol is healthy, and the governance process around the protocol is functioning, but a decision undertaken is sufficiently poor that it kills the protocol.
death by mismanagement.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by fatal flaw.definition: A mode of protocol failure where a discovered flaw cannot be repaired or causes irrecoverable damage, such as security vulnerabilities or foundational design flaws.
death by fatal flaw.context: Death by fatal flaw: when a flaw is discovered in the protocol that cannot be repaired or causes irrecoverable damage, such as a security vulnerability or a foundational design choice with unforeseen consequences
death by fatal flaw.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by external threat.definition: A mode of protocol failure caused by regulatory threats or existential risks so significant they kill the protocol through chilling effects or direct bans.
death by external threat.context: Death by external threat: when a regulatory threat or existential risk becomes so significant that the protocol dies from chilling effect/ direct ban
death by external threat.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

protocol-euthanasia.definition: The deliberate discontinuation or abandonment of a protocol by its decision-makers as a controlled end-of-life decision.
protocol-euthanasia.context: Death by shutdown: when the decision-makers of the protocol choose to discontinue it or abandon the system, sometimes called protocol-euthanasia
protocol-euthanasia.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by substrate failure.definition: A mode of protocol failure when a necessary foundational dependency of the protocol fails, causing cascading failures of systems that depend on it.
death by substrate failure.context: Death by substrate failure: when some necessary foundation of the protocol fails by any means, ie., if tcp/ip fails, many things which depend on it would fail also
death by substrate failure.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by access failure.definition: A mode of protocol failure when the protocol can no longer be accessed due to failure of external systems that provide access, independent of the protocol itself.
death by access failure.context: Death by access failure: when the protocol can no longer be accessed, for reasons external to itself, ie. if web browsers fail, http is likely to also fail
death by access failure.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by competition.definition: A mode of protocol failure where a new protocol better meets the needs previously served by an existing protocol, making the original obsolete.
death by competition.context: Death by competition: when a new protocol arises that better meets the needs met by the previous protocol
death by competition.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by sufficient change.definition: A mode of protocol failure where accumulated changes transform a protocol so thoroughly that it can no longer be considered the original protocol.
death by sufficient change.context: Death by sufficient change: when a protocol has changed so much that it can no longer be said to be the original protocol
death by sufficient change.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by oblivion.definition: A mode of protocol failure where a protocol is abandoned, forgotten, misunderstood, or not propagated for further use without deliberate coordinated maintenance.
death by oblivion.context: Death by oblivion: when the protocol is abandoned, forgotten, misunderstood, or is not propagated for further use without deliberate coordinated intent
death by oblivion.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death by rebellion.definition: A mode of protocol failure caused by a coordinated popular campaign or rebellion against a protocol that results in its death.
death by rebellion.context: Death by rebellion: when a rebellion or coordinated popular campaign against a protocol causes its death
death by rebellion.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

meme war.definition: A coordinated campaign of persuasion and non-compliance tactics undertaken by those without direct decision-making power to undermine support for a protocol.
meme war.context: If you are a lone agent, not a decision-maker of the protocol, you will need to undertake a meme war
meme war.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

lifecycle of a world.definition: The progression of states a world moves through, including pre-alive, alive, dying, and afterlife phases, with possible pathways for revival or spawning of new worlds.
lifecycle of a world.context: There is more than one path through the lifecycle. A world that is not fully shut down can sometimes come back to life. A world in its afterlife can spawn new living worlds.
lifecycle of a world.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

afterlife.definition: The state of a protocol or world after its death, where secondary ways to engage with it may still exist, or from which new living worlds can be spawned.
afterlife.context: worlds which are fully shut down but there are secondary ways to engage
afterlife.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

protocol death registry.definition: An official record and memorial system documenting the deaths of protocols, overseen by the Order as a notarial function.
protocol death registry.context: Acting as notary for the Protocol Death Registry... Stained glass window proposals for the Protocol Death Registry
protocol death registry.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

life-locations of worlds.definition: The various sites and spaces—both digital and social—where a world's existence is maintained, including subreddits, fanfiction, social media, and events.
life-locations of worlds.context: The life of the world may not be *in* the world... subreddits, fanfiction, social media mentions
life-locations of worlds.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

stillbirth.definition: A mode of protocological death where a protocol never achieves actual lived existence despite being founded or designed.
stillbirth.context: Stillbirth: one might ask, did this protocol ever live?
stillbirth.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

protocol archive.definition: A curated collection of records, documentation, and memorial materials related to a deceased protocol, maintained in accordance with the protocol's wishes.
protocol archive.context: Shepherding and maintaining protocol archives, in accordance with the wishes of the deceased
protocol archive.source: Founding memorabilia from the Order of Protocological Death

death-as-a-process.definition: The understanding that death is not a binary transition but a protracted process (dying) that may result in a liminal state between alive and dead with possible disagreement about relative liveness or deadness.
death-as-a-process.context: First, death­as­a­process: death is not a simple binary transition, instead it is a process (dying) that may result in a protracted liminal state between alive and dead.

death-as-a-decision.definition: The understanding that death is not a given or clear natural fact, but instead a decision similar to a diagnosis, with domain-specific criteria determined by technology, authority, and culture.
death-as-a-decision.context: Twice Dead: Organ Transplants and the Reinvention of Death... Second death, ritual understandings of a liminal state between life and death, and changing medical and legal practices are all examples that de­center death from a fixed event that happens to a body... into a social decision-making process.

consensus death.definition: The point at which a world reaches agreement about its deadness, typically marked by a decision undertaken by an authority or ritual, ending the liminal dying process.
consensus death.context: At some point in the lifecycle, the liminal state ends—in the case of an MMO, the end usually looks like its developer going out of business or making the decision to no longer maintain the servers—and the world reaches consensus death.

liminal state.definition: A transitional period between being alive and dead where a world or entity exists in ontological uncertainty, characterized by possible disagreement about its relative liveness or deadness.
liminal state.context: Many MMOs that have lost their rich player community... are better described as being in a liminal state between alive and dead—something like a protracted dying.

worlding.definition: The process by which platforms, places, books, games, or philosophical movements generate living ecosystems through the participation and attention of their participants.
worlding.context: A world grows on top of a protocol when the protocol lives. Platforms, places, books, TV shows, video games, or philosophical movements can also generate worlds.

second death.definition: A social death that occurs when an individual's name or memory is no longer known among the living, particularly relevant in digital contexts where this has been complicated by persistent digital records.
second death.context: 'Second death,' however, acknowledges that 'second death' has been complicated by the digital.

rite of passage.definition: A ritual transition from one state to another consisting of three phases: separation (from the previous state), liminality (being between states), and incorporation (into the new state).
rite of passage.context: In Celebrations of Death: The Anthropology of Mortuary Ritual, Peter Metcalf and Richard Huntington use the framework of 'rites of passage' to examine death rituals.

secondary processing.definition: A funerary practice involving an initial ritual, followed by a lengthy intermediary period of months to years, after which the corpse is exhumed and a further ritual concludes the death process.
secondary processing.context: Metcalf and Huntington follow this with an extended analysis of cultures where there is secondary processing of the corpse, namely, an initial ritual, followed by a lengthy intermediary period consisting of months to as much as five years, after which the corpse is exhumed and a further ritual concludes the death process.

death-decider.definition: An authority or organization given the power to make binding decisions about whether something is dead, establishing consensus death through decision-making protocols or rituals.
death-decider.context: Who has been given authority to decide that something is dead; what rituals or protocols are undertaken to cement its deadness? In the human context, doctors, lawyers, and sometimes religious figures play these roles. In the context of worlds like games or social media platforms, these roles are performed by a company or organization.

order of protocological death.definition: An emerging or proposed independent body that tracks and documents the deaths of decentralized protocols and blockchain projects, analogous to medical and legal authorities in human death determination.
order of protocological death.context: One can imagine these initiatives to track dead coins as an emerging Order of Proto cological Death, perhaps becoming an independent body the way the medical and legal profession become arbiters of human death.

death indicator.definition: A measurable criterion used to diagnose whether a protocol or blockchain is dead, including metrics such as trading volume, website status, node activity, and social media presence.
death indicator.context: Already, the death indicators used by the deadcoin lists are like a doctor inspecting first for an absence of swallow reflex, then for no eye response to light, and no limb movement on painful stimulus.

difficulty bomb.definition: A mechanism in the Ethereum protocol designed to make mining progressively harder at a specified time, forcing a transition to proof of stake or requiring protocol updates to maintain chain functionality.
difficulty bomb.context: Another example of existential stress in the peer-to-peer context is what was named 'the difficulty bomb' mechanism in Ethereum. Initially written into the protocol as part of the planned switch to proof of stake, the difficulty bomb was a feature where at a given point in time it would become exponentially more difficult to find correct blocks.

proof of stake.definition: A consensus mechanism for blockchain systems where validators are chosen to create new blocks based on their stake in the network, in contrast to proof of work systems that require computational power.
proof of stake.context: Initially written into the protocol as part of the planned switch to proof of stake, the difficulty bomb was a feature where at a given point in time it would become exponentially more difficult to find correct blocks using the old proof of work mining system.

autonomous world.definition: A blockchain-based gaming world that operates as a decentralized ecosystem where participants inhabit worlds with their own boundaries and rulesets that are not controlled by a central authority.
autonomous world.context: A related case would be autonomous worlds, a framework for blockchain gaming proposed by 0xPARC. The way 0xPARC characterizes a world has much in common with the way we do here.

fantasy of perfect capture.definition: The mistaken assumption that backing up all data of a digital world—its software, code, and server data—fully captures the essential meaning and nature of that world.
fantasy of perfect capture.context: The report calls this the fantasy of perfect capture: while we can back up the data that encompasses a game, this doesn't capture what the game really is.

memorial.definition: A form of documentation or testimony to what cannot be fully archived, serving as a compression of technology and a testament to the uncapturable, too big, or symbolically significant aspects of a world.
memorial.context: It's useful to contrast dumb storage with a memorial. With dumb storage, the fantasy of recreating the thing being archived can exist... No such pretense persists with a memorial. Instead perhaps, a memorial exists as a testament to what cannot be archived.

hyperthymesia.definition: A neurological condition characterized by the inability to forget one's past, resulting in highly accurate autobiographical memory that is associated with negative effects including depression and relationship difficulties.
hyperthymesia.context: Highly accurate autobiographical memory, or hyperthymesia—the inability to forget one's past—is associated with negative effects, including depression and difficulty in personal relationships.

peripheral forum.definition: Community spaces outside a protocol or world where discussion about that protocol or world takes place, serving as an important indicator of the world's continued health and life.
peripheral forum.context: Any sufficiently healthy world will spawn activity in peripheral forums where the protocol is discussed. It will spread and animate spaces outside itself. The life of the world is not only in the world.

avatar.definition: A digital representation of a participant within a world or protocol through which they interact, accumulate experiences, and build relationships with other participants.
avatar.context: A world is an ecosystem of avatars, grown through their time and attention.

feedback loop.definition: A mechanism in a protocol that communicates outcomes and results back to participants so they can understand whether their actions succeeded or failed.
feedback loop.context: No (or hidden) feedback loop; Lack of consequences for failed outcomes; Outcomes aren't visible to participants.
feedback loop.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

evaluative metrics.definition: Measurable criteria that determine whether a protocol has succeeded or failed, and whether these metrics are appropriate to the protocol's intended purpose.
evaluative metrics.context: No evaluative metrics, or wrong metrics prioritized; Success outcomes are randomized or ambiguously defined.
evaluative metrics.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

happy path.definition: The straightforward, optimal sequence of steps through a protocol that leads directly to successful completion without detours or complications.
happy path.context: No happy path to follow; Protocol increases the number of decisions that participant must make.
happy path.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

edge cases.definition: Unusual or exceptional scenarios and conditions that a protocol must handle, distinct from the standard or expected use cases.
edge cases.context: Too many edge cases addressed at once.

branching.definition: The ability of a protocol to offer multiple pathways or decision points that allow participants to follow different routes based on their circumstances.
branching.context: No branching or forking of use cases.

user error.definition: Mistakes that participants can make when following a protocol due to ambiguous instructions or multiple ways to interpret or implement the required steps.
user error.context: User error is possible (multiple ways to "plug it in").

participant agency.definition: The degree of control and decision-making power that a protocol grants to its users in determining their own outcomes and actions.
participant agency.context: Maintaining a high level of agency limits their ability to manage increasingly complex tasks. Balanced power between protocol and participant.

recursive nested protocols.definition: Protocols that contain other protocols within them, layered in a self-referential manner that increases complexity and can trap participants in circular dependencies.
recursive nested protocols.context: Recursive, nested protocols. Protocol's complexity is sprawling, with multiple dead ends.

whirlpools.definition: Circular patterns within protocols where participants become caught in loops or cycles with no mechanism for escape or resolution.
whirlpools.context: Participants can get trapped in endless loops or 'whirlpools' with no resolution.
whirlpools.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

redundant protocols.definition: Multiple protocols that attempt to solve the same problem, creating conflict and confusion among participants who must choose between them.
redundant protocols.context: Multiple protocols exist that attempt to solve the same problem. Redundant protocols create conflict and confusion.

protocol goodness.definition: The quality or success of a protocol measured against archetypes representing different distributions of power and complexity between the protocol system and its participants.
protocol goodness.context: 3 archetypes of protocol 'goodness': Kafka — failure archetype; Bartleby — failure archetype; Whitehead — success archetype.
protocol goodness.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

kafka — failure archetype.definition: A category of protocol failure characterized by overwhelming complexity, recursive nesting, and dead ends that trap participants in an inescapable maze they cannot understand.
kafka — failure archetype.context: Kafka — failure archetype: 'I can't find my way round in this darkness.' Recursive, nested protocols; Protocol holds too much power; Protocol's complexity is sprawling, with multiple dead ends.
kafka — failure archetype.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

bartleby — failure archetype.definition: A category of protocol failure where participants lack viable alternatives and face such high costs of participation or defection that they are effectively trapped with no choice.
bartleby — failure archetype.context: Bartleby — failure archetype: 'I would prefer not to.' No market or alternatives exist; High cost to participate, with no other options available; Significant costs incurred if participants defect.
bartleby — failure archetype.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

whitehead — success archetype.definition: A model of protocol goodness based on balanced power between protocol and participant, where the protocol handles complexity so participants can accomplish more without consciously managing every detail.
whitehead — success archetype.context: Whitehead — success archetype: 'Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.' Balanced power between protocol and participant.
whitehead — success archetype.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

recursive, nested protocols.definition: Protocols that are embedded within other protocols at multiple levels, creating layers of complexity that can trap participants in endless loops without clear resolution.
recursive, nested protocols.context: Recursive, nested protocols; Protocol holds too much power; Protocol's complexity is sprawling, with multiple dead ends; Participants can get trapped in endless loops or 'whirlpools' with no resolution.
recursive, nested protocols.source: Kafka Index: Evaluative criteria for identifying bad protocols

killswitch protocol.definition: An engineered mechanism or set of rules that enables the intentional stopping or overriding of a complex system to prevent severe or unforeseen consequences.
killswitch protocol.context: Enter the killswitch: an engineered acknowledgment and accommodation of severe and unforeseen consequences. We are so confident that something wildly awful may happen, we engineer mechanisms to stop the entire system, including systems whose continued processes are ostensibly value-producing!
killswitch protocol.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

recursive override function.definition: The self-referential quality of killswitches that allows a system to check and constrain its own processes and those of its participants, especially powerful actors.
recursive override function.context: The recursive override function of killswitches that we have described is more ubiquitous than the term might suggest. Our systems frequently require the presence of a method to prevent internal processes from spiraling out of control.
recursive override function.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

system death.definition: The intentional cessation or termination of a complex system's operations, either permanently or temporarily, as a failsafe mechanism.
system death.context: Both considerations centrally motivate our analysis here: we can engineer complex systems that can spiral out of control with staggering negative consequences. Industrialized society, then, needs an overriding failsafe that can stop the system.
system death.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

killswitch governance.definition: The set of decision-making structures and authority arrangements that determine who controls when and how a killswitch is exercised, ranging from fully automated to fully democratic.
killswitch governance.context: Given how common killswitches are in human engineered systems, including digital communities, protocols have naturally emerged to govern their exercise. A killswitch should not be lightly engaged and, in some instances, cannot be reversed once the button has been pushed.
killswitch governance.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

reification (of protocol).definition: The process of encoding a protocol into automated, algorithmic triggers that remove human discretion from its execution.
reification (of protocol).context: At the one end of the continuum of governance choices for killswitches is the total reification of the protocol into an automated set of triggers. While this removes such an override from the control of a central authority, it also removes it from the control of those within the system that is being stopped.
reification (of protocol).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

protocol awareness.definition: The degree to which participants in a system consciously understand and recognize the protocols governing their behavior, as opposed to following them implicitly or unconsciously.
protocol awareness.context: But a killswitch's existence (and resultant responsibility borne by the stakeholders of the system being killed) may itself encourage protocol awareness. However, within complex systems, there are no panaceas, only solutions that pose tradeoffs.
protocol awareness.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

circuit breaker function.definition: A specific application of a killswitch that allows temporary suspension or revocation of system access or processes, typically invoked to prevent cascading failures.
circuit breaker function.context: If the Superset Trust deems data uses or revenue to be at odds with member interests, it can exercise the circuit breaker function and batch revoke member consent to continue collecting or using the data.
circuit breaker function.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

nested killswitches.definition: A hierarchical structure of multiple killswitches operating at different system levels, where specific functions or the entire system can be subject to override depending on triggers.
nested killswitches.context: Together these abilities display a characteristic noteworthy of nested killswitches: specific functions or the whole system can be subject to an override, depending on the trigger.
nested killswitches.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

attack vector.definition: A potential pathway or vulnerability through which adversarial actors can exploit a system, often created or amplified by the presence of concentrated value or control mechanisms.
attack vector.context: Exposure to financialization or other tradeable within-system goods creates attack vectors. These vectors are naturally pursued by self-interested agents within the system to the degree that the original system is successful in capturing value.
attack vector.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

protocolized purpose.definition: The formal, explicit encoding of a system's intended goals and functions into structured rules and procedures that guide participant behavior.
protocolized purpose.context: The intent of a human-designed system cannot be realized absent the context of a protocolized purpose.
protocolized purpose.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

extraction (versus apportionment).definition: A characterization of how protocols relate to the value generated by system participants: extractive protocols concentrate benefits away from participants, while apportionment protocols distribute benefits among them.
extraction (versus apportionment).context: As protocols govern complex human systems, they have consequences that people naturally seek to channel or avoid, depending on individual costs and benefits. Setting aside total ignorance of the control systems to which we are subject leaves systems that either extract or apportion the efforts of the individuals within them.
extraction (versus apportionment).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

willingness (of protocol participants).definition: The degree to which participants voluntarily and consciously accept and follow a protocol, as opposed to reluctantly resisting it.
willingness (of protocol participants).context: The latter class of system participants tends to be more productive. By the same token, however, being 'fully conscious' of a protocol is, in some instances, antithetical to what a protocol does. Routinizing human behavior into a protocol can be characterized as a form of forgetting.
willingness (of protocol participants).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

coordination equilibrium.definition: A stable state in a system where the incentives and behaviors of independent participants align toward a common or mutually beneficial outcome.
coordination equilibrium.context: Our systems frequently require the presence of a method to prevent internal processes from spiraling out of control, to align incentives between system participants, to create a coordinating equilibrium among independent players, or to obtain a more democratic means of governance.
coordination equilibrium.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

legitimacy (of system governance).definition: The quality of being recognized as rightful and justified by system participants, which increases their voluntary cooperation and reduces reliance on enforcement.
legitimacy (of system governance).context: In private systems where exit costs are sufficiently low, oppressive governance cannot survive in the face of competing systems that offer participants more representative alternatives. The extent to which a given human system needs to cultivate legitimacy ultimately depends on the purpose that system is designed to achieve.
legitimacy (of system governance).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

high trust environment.definition: A system context where participants believe others will follow agreements and act in good faith, enabling more efficient and productive coordination.
high trust environment.context: The decision to distribute killswitch control among all assembly line employees is considered to be a significant input to Toyota's success compared to the U.S. auto industry over the same time period. It is likely that this killswitch protocol could only operate in the high trust environment that the company culture created.
high trust environment.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

meta-strategies.definition: Behaviors or actions aimed at winning or succeeding by exploiting the rules or structure of a system rather than directly achieving the intended object-level goals.
meta-strategies.context: A discretionary disqualification serves as the threatened killswitch in these contexts that serves to align players' incentives to contest within the rules, as opposed to skirting them in ways system designers never intended. Any competition will naturally invite players to pursue value at the margins.
meta-strategies.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

endogenous need (for killswitches).definition: The internal, self-generating requirement that emerges within complex systems for mechanisms to stop or override their own processes, due to unintended consequences.
endogenous need (for killswitches).context: Most recursively, even as fundamental of a ruleset as a constitution must contemplate its own means of amendment. Thus, the beneficial effects that institutional design provides in coordinating collective action in complex social orders carries its own endogenous need for killswitches.
endogenous need (for killswitches).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

distributed control.definition: A governance arrangement where decision-making authority and power are spread among multiple participants or entities rather than concentrated in a single authority.
distributed control.context: In the cool new digital frontier involving transparent and distributed governance of data and coordinated units of account, we're seeing increasing automation of components of organizations, as well as governance contexts that facilitate greater distributed control of system components, including killswitches.
distributed control.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

value capture.definition: The ability or act of concentrating the benefits or returns generated by a system within particular actors or entities, often at the expense of other participants.
value capture.context: If the only cost of representative killswitch governance was efficiency, design of killswitch protocols would be far easier than it actually is. But in addition to coordination costs, these killswitches carry a far greater risk: distributed input on killswitch protocols increases the vulnerability to adversarial exercise of the killswitch.
value capture.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

constructivist intent.definition: The specific goals and consequences that designers deliberately intend a system or protocol to produce.
constructivist intent.context: Limits to constructivist intent within complex systems means killswitches will in important instances fail to fully restrain the system's processes or carry unintended consequences when they do manage to do so.
constructivist intent.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

public good (in daos and collective syst.term: public good (in DAOs and collective systems)
public good (in daos and collective syst.definition: A benefit or outcome that advantages a community or collective as a whole, though its definition and boundaries are often contested and difficult to specify precisely.
public good (in daos and collective syst.context: At a more structural level, the issue of clearly defining the 'public good' for a given system itself outstrips the ability to define all margins of this good. In the case of DAOs, certain components of organizational processes lack sufficient resolution for algorithmic reconciliation.
public good (in daos and collective syst.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

trustlessness.definition: A system design approach that minimizes or eliminates the need for participants to trust one another or central authorities by using algorithmic enforcement and transparency.
trustlessness.context: Trust concentrates risk while trustlessness can distribute risk. Yet both high trust and low trust approaches to protocolization can create attack vectors.
trustlessness.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

object-level goals (versus meta-level).definition: The direct, primary purposes of a system or competition, as opposed to the higher-order rules and frameworks that govern how those goals are pursued.
object-level goals (versus meta-level).context: Indeed, an early AI told to 'win' a racing video game obtained maximum points by capturing valuable side items, but lost spectacularly due to the system designers forgetting to enshrine winning the race itself as a primary objective!
object-level goals (versus meta-level).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

common pool resource (or common treasury.definition: A shared fund or asset that multiple participants can access or benefit from, which creates collective action problems and potential attack vectors.
common pool resource (or common treasury.context: DAOs frequently aggregate funds for community public goods, but simultaneously create a pot of money that is both an attack vector and an often-undesired killswitch for the DAO itself. A common pool of money over which to coordinate can become a DAO's fatal flaw.
common pool resource (or common treasury.source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

representation (in governance).definition: The degree to which decision-making processes give voice and influence to the interests and preferences of diverse system participants.
representation (in governance).context: Checks on the power of the governors tends to induce more representative governance and, therefore, more willing and conscious participation. The representativity of coordination comes at the cost of efficiency, at least with respect to the cost of reaching the decision itself.
representation (in governance).source: Killswitch Protocols: Or On Engineering Recursive System Death

information structure.definition: The arrangement and distribution of knowledge within a protocol, determining who knows what information and when they know it.
information structure.context: What is the information structure of your protocol? Who knows what, when? Who forgets what, and when?
information structure.source: Protocol Kit Package 2: Memory and Time

temporality.definition: The characteristic ways a protocol structures, embodies, and changes through time, including its temporal rhythms and cycles.
temporality.context: What is the temporality associated with your protocol? How does it change in time? How does it embody time?
temporality.source: Protocol Kit Package 2: Memory and Time

atoms.definition: The minimal, irreducible material or computational units within a protocol that embody time and memory and form the foundation of protocol operation.
atoms.context: What atoms embody time and memory? Where in space are those atoms located, and how are they arranged and governed?
atoms.source: Protocol Kit Package 2: Memory and Time

memory as orientation.definition: A framework for understanding how protocols use memory not merely for storage but as a means of navigating, organizing, and orienting action through time.
memory as orientation.context: Anchoring this exploration, we have Kei Kreutler's essay, Memory as Orientation
memory as orientation.source: Protocol Kit Package 2: Memory and Time

spatialities and materialities.definition: The physical and spatial dimensions underlying a protocol, including where information is stored, how it is arranged, and what material substrates embody it.
spatialities and materialities.context: What are the spatialities and materialities associated with memory and temporality in your protocol?
spatialities and materialities.source: Protocol Kit Package 2: Memory and Time

death-and-resurrection liminal passage.definition: A transitional threshold state that systems or games enter when they approach natural conclusion, characterized by both ending and potential renewal.
death-and-resurrection liminal passage.context: When a game converges towards a natural conclusion, you enter a death-and-resurrection liminal passage.

bitrot.definition: The gradual decay and obsolescence of digital information and systems over time, particularly concerning how information degrades online.
bitrot.context: Part of the rationale is to manage bitrot and other digital death-and-decay phenomena.

killswitch.definition: A mechanism in protocols that allows for system termination or disabling, with specific design tradeoffs for system architects.
killswitch.context: In 'The Killswitch Effect,' Eric Alston, Seth Killian, and Garette David, we have a detailed exploration of the dynamics of protocols that feature killswitches and the tradeoffs they induce for system designers.

swarm protocols.definition: Protocols that coordinate collective action through distributed, self-organizing mechanisms, as applied to understanding mass political movements and formations.
swarm protocols.context: we have an account of the titular protests through the lens of Rafael Fernandez's theories of protocols and swarms

institutional death and resurrection dyn.definition: Patterns of how institutions and systems undergo cycles of ending and renewal, particularly in relation to ownership, enclosure, and commons structures.
institutional death and resurrection dyn.context: Trent Van Epps' essay on enclosure movements in software...rounds out this collection of writings on what we might call institutional death and resurrection dynamics.

urban protocol patterns.definition: Recurring design patterns and rule structures that emerge in or govern urban spaces and city-level coordination.
urban protocol patterns.context: the final patterns from Drew Austin's collection of urban protocol patterns

information architecture for dense hyper.definition: A framework for organizing and managing complex information relationships online, designed to handle intricate interconnections and manage digital decay gracefully.
information architecture for dense hyper.context: Dorian Taylor explains the reasoning and philosophy behind Intertwingler, a web information architecture for dense hypermedia.

time machines.definition: Physical or conceptual devices—ranging from low-tech objects to digital systems—that enable revisiting of people and places no longer present through memory practices.
time machines.context: Ranging from low-tech objects to never-before-seen devices, our new time machines bring ancient memorial protocols to modern memory artists.
time machines.source: Welcome to the New Time Machines Working Group

memorial protocols.definition: Ancient or traditional procedures and rituals specifically designed to preserve and transmit memory across generations and communities.
memorial protocols.context: Ranging from low-tech objects to never-before-seen devices, our new time machines bring ancient memorial protocols to modern memory artists.
memorial protocols.source: Welcome to the New Time Machines Working Group

procedural memory.definition: Memory engaged through explicit step-by-step instructions or procedures rather than passive storage, emphasizing the active practice of remembering.
procedural memory.context: these instructions for how to procedurally remember serve three purposes. Firstly, they help revive and reorient us in the present to the art of memory.
procedural memory.source: Welcome to the New Time Machines Working Group

arts of memory.definition: Traditional disciplines and techniques, historically developed and passed down through generations, for systematically training and enhancing human memory capacities.
arts of memory.context: For ages, the arts of memory were rigorously developed and passed down from generation to generation.
arts of memory.source: Welcome to the New Time Machines Working Group

plural voting mechanisms.definition: Voting systems that build on traditional linear and quadratic voting by considering the relationships between voters and weighting their preferences accordingly to reward diverse group consensus.
plural voting mechanisms.context: Plural voting mechanisms build on traditional linear and quadratic voting mechanisms by considering the relationships between voters and weighting their preferences accordingly. The goal is to reward diverse group consensus, ensuring that decision-making reflects a broader range of perspectives while preventing dominance by heavily aligned voters.

relational identity.definition: Information about the relationships and group memberships of voters that is used to weight their votes in plural voting mechanisms, which can change over time and significantly impact results based on how dimensions are chosen.
relational identity.context: Most examples of real-world plural voting have used a snapshot of relational identity. Adding temporality to plural voting is complex, especially if participants themselves are in control of these changes.

connection-oriented cluster match (cocm).definition: An experimental plural voting mechanism designed to assess protocol effectiveness in diverse, practical scenarios through simulations and real-world tests.
connection-oriented cluster match (cocm).context: The centerpiece was our own experiment into Connection-Oriented Cluster Match (COCM). We planned to use simulations and real-world tests to assess the protocol's effectiveness in diverse, practical scenarios.

calibration.definition: The careful tuning and adjustment of plural voting mechanisms to function optimally for a specific implementation context, which requires deep understanding of how the mechanisms work.
calibration.context: Even where implementers are well-intentioned, correct calibration of these mechanisms requires a deep and nuanced understanding of how they function.

plurality vs. authority tension.definition: The central contradiction in plural voting systems wherein reducing the influence of powerful voting blocs requires top-down judgments that can themselves bias results and concentrate power.
plurality vs. authority tension.context: Although plural mechanisms aim to reduce the influence of a powerful voting bloc, successfully implementing these mechanisms requires a lot of top-down judgments which can bias results.

pairwise quadratic voting.definition: A mechanism designed to avoid top-down identity decisions in plural voting by generating correlations between voters through pairwise comparisons, though its real-world applicability remains unclear.
pairwise quadratic voting.context: Attempts to avoid top-down identity decisions, such as pairwise quadratic voting, are interesting but seem incompatible with real-world voting scenarios (particularly in DAOs).

anti-correlation modifiers.definition: Adjustments applied to plural voting mechanisms to reduce the impact of highly aligned voters and prevent dominance of particular voting blocs.
anti-correlation modifiers.context: It is unclear how to handle relational identity over time. E.g., at what point should groupings newly generated by the mechanism be subject to the same anti-correlation modifiers.

diverse group consensus.definition: Decision outcomes that reflect input from and agreement across a broad range of perspectives rather than being dominated by aligned voter blocks.
diverse group consensus.context: The goal is to reward diverse group consensus, ensuring that decision-making reflects a broader range of perspectives while preventing dominance by heavily aligned voters.

capture (in voting mechanisms).definition: The vulnerability of voting protocols to manipulation or control by organized actors, which requires careful implementation to resist.
capture (in voting mechanisms).context: It's not clear that this shift in power always makes things more plural, and most are still eminently capturable without care.

identity dimension.definition: A specific category or aspect of relational identity used to group voters in plural voting systems, the choice of which can significantly affect voting outcomes.
identity dimension.context: Poor choice of identity dimensions can significantly skew results.

surprising consensus.definition: Unexpected or counterintuitive agreement that emerges from plural voting mechanisms designed to surface perspectives that might otherwise remain hidden.
surprising consensus.context: Plurality often aims to surface surprising consensus, which LLM-based AI analysis stifles.

distancing layer.definition: A structural or procedural element in plural voting that creates psychological or temporal distance between participants, helping to defuse conflict and enable collaboration.
distancing layer.context: Much of this success may be due to factors such as novelty and the fact they add a distancing layer to defuse the conflict.

problem pattern.definition: A recurring challenge or constraint in urban space that affects multiple participants and creates demand for coordination solutions.
problem pattern.context: Problem Pattern: Opportunities for local small businesses to engage in physical retail are often constrained by regulations and licensing requirements.
problem pattern.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

positive externalities.definition: Beneficial effects generated by locally situated retail businesses that extend beyond the direct transaction to benefit the broader neighborhood community.
positive externalities.context: Depriving neighborhood communities of the positive externalities that locally situated retail businesses offer.
positive externalities.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

microenterprise home kitchen operations.definition: A regulatory framework allowing individuals to legally operate licensed food businesses out of their homes with reduced capital costs and administrative requirements.
microenterprise home kitchen operations.context: In 2018 California legalized 'microenterprise home kitchen operations,' allowing anyone to run a licensed restaurant out of their home.
microenterprise home kitchen operations.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

serendipitous encounters.definition: Unplanned, chance meetings between individuals that occur within a shared geographic space, creating opportunities for social connection.
serendipitous encounters.context: Many city dwellers complain that they do not know their neighbors and suffer from a dearth of opportunities to meet new people outside of narrow domains such as work and school through serendipitous encounters.
serendipitous encounters.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

neighborhood serendipity protocols.definition: Digitally-augmented systems designed to increase the frequency and variety of unplanned social interactions among residents at the neighborhood geographic scale.
neighborhood serendipity protocols.context: There remains an opportunity to use localized social media (or something like it) to support a broader range of in person interactions beyond dating, with a particular focus on the neighborhood as a meaningful geographic scope.
neighborhood serendipity protocols.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

localized social media.definition: Digital platforms that facilitate social interaction and connection specifically scoped to geographic neighborhoods rather than broader networks.
localized social media.context: There remains an opportunity to use localized social media (or something like it) to support a broader range of in person interactions beyond dating, with a particular focus on the neighborhood as a meaningful geographic scope.
localized social media.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

digitally augmented social interaction.definition: Face-to-face social encounters that are initiated or facilitated through digital technologies and location-based data.
digitally augmented social interaction.context: Serendipitous interactions with one's neighbors are occurrences that apps still offer the potential to encourage through digitally augmented social interaction.
digitally augmented social interaction.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

participants.definition: The key actors and stakeholder groups involved in implementing and benefiting from a given protocol pattern.
participants.context: Participants: Small business owners (existing and potential) and Individual neighborhood residents and visitors.
participants.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

infrastructure.definition: The physical systems, facilities, and technical platforms required to enable a protocol pattern to function effectively.
infrastructure.context: Infrastructure: Housing that can accommodate small business operations; marketing infrastructure (in lieu of street-facing storefronts), adequate licensing processes and Mobile apps that facilitate localized interaction.
infrastructure.source: A Protocol Pattern Language for Urban Space

hardened shorelines.definition: Infrastructure-based coastal protection strategies that use rigid engineered structures to prevent water from entering urban areas and maintain static, unchanging waterfront boundaries.
hardened shorelines.context: Hardened shorelines and/or green infrastructure strategies are selected to reduce the presence of water in cities, preserve a static shoreline, and frequently disconnect communities from their coastlines.
hardened shorelines.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

green infrastructure strategies.definition: Nature-based coastal adaptation approaches such as bioswales and wetlands designed to manage flooding while maintaining some ecological function.
green infrastructure strategies.context: Hardened shorelines and/or green infrastructure strategies are selected to reduce the presence of water in cities, preserve a static shoreline, and frequently disconnect communities from their coastlines.
green infrastructure strategies.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

adaptive shorelines.definition: Waterfront management approaches that embrace dynamic change and ongoing adjustment rather than attempting to maintain fixed, static conditions.
adaptive shorelines.context: We aimed to identify additional patterns—protocols—of activism, engagement, and use cases that enable vibrant and adaptive shorelines.
adaptive shorelines.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

risk-based framing.definition: An approach to coastal adaptation planning that prioritizes protecting existing capital investments and measures potential harm primarily through economic calculations of property and financial loss.
risk-based framing.context: The risk is a key calculation in adaptation planning, and nearly all global governments measure risk through economic calculations that value property, human life, and other concerns through the lens of finance.
risk-based framing.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

pulsing landscapes.definition: Waterfront environments that naturally experience regular cycles of inundation and drying, accepting seasonal or periodic flooding as an inherent characteristic rather than an anomaly.
pulsing landscapes.context: The fiction that land along shorelines remains dry is a modern concept. People have been living within pulsing landscapes forever, accepting and adapting to seasonal flooding through floating and raised infrastructure.
pulsing landscapes.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

cultural relationship to water.definition: The collective social attitudes, beliefs, and behavioral patterns that shape how communities understand, value, and interact with water in their lived environments.
cultural relationship to water.context: In order to truly change our approach to coastal adaptation, we need to go beyond grey and green infrastructure that mitigates flooding. We need to shift our expectations and our cultural relationship to water.
cultural relationship to water.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Floating Urban Waterways

broken public engagement process.definition: Ineffective mechanisms for community participation in planning that fail to address citizens' actual concerns and do not reflect public input in decision outcomes.
broken public engagement process.context: We encountered two problems: a broken public engagement process, and a shared focus on risk among both planners and communities.
broken public engagement process.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

perception of wetness.definition: The public understanding of water presence in urban environments as a threat or risk to be eliminated, shaped primarily by negative flood experiences rather than alternative values.
perception of wetness.context: The most common experience that shapes people's awareness or thinking about water where they live is flooding—often in storms. These negative experiences contribute to a public perception of 'wetness' as a risk for urban life.
perception of wetness.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

downstream impacts.definition: Unintended negative consequences of protective infrastructure that displace hazards to other, often economically disadvantaged areas rather than eliminating them.
downstream impacts.context: Seawalls create many negative downstream impacts, pushing water to less protected (often poorer) areas, create erosion, interrupting how tidal harbors flush pollutants.
downstream impacts.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

nature-based solutions.definition: Adaptation strategies that leverage natural systems and ecological processes to manage coastal flooding and erosion.
nature-based solutions.context: Adaptation planning has improved—long-term, sea-level rise projections and nature-based solutions are now widely considered—but the focus on protection and risk hasn't changed.
nature-based solutions.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

static shoreline.definition: A waterfront boundary maintained at a fixed location through engineered protection, preventing natural migration or adjustment of the coastline.
static shoreline.context: Hardened shorelines and/or green infrastructure strategies are selected to reduce the presence of water in cities, preserve a static shoreline, and frequently disconnect communities from their coastlines.
static shoreline.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

informal projects.definition: Community-led or grassroots adaptation initiatives outside formal governmental planning processes that can shift cultural perceptions and behaviors around water.
informal projects.context: We explored improving public engagement processes, better equipping communities to participate in them, and finally focused on informal projects that shift perceptions about living with water.
informal projects.source: Shoreline Adaptations to Flooding in Urban Waterways

summer of protocols.definition: An initiative or research program focused on the systematic study and development of protocols as coordination mechanisms.
summer of protocols.context: Summer of Protocols summerofprotocols.com inquiries :: hello@summerofprotocols.com

death protocols.definition: Structured procedures and timelines established by a platform to manage user transition and data preservation when a service is being shut down.
death protocols.context: When Google took action in June 2014 and declared it was pulling the plug, Orkut's death protocols were shared with the user base: they had three months of use, three months to export their photos to Google+, two years to export their data.
death protocols.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

protocol of adaptation.definition: A formal set of procedures that marks and manages the transition of a digital system from one operational state to another, typically from active to archived or inactive.
protocol of adaptation.context: The community archive had a specific protocol of adaptation from one life state to another, which cemented the status change from living to dead: no new content could be generated.
protocol of adaptation.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

good death.definition: A planned, transparent, and respectful shutdown of a digital service that provides adequate time and clear procedures for users to preserve their data and memories.
good death.context: Orkut had a good death—its archive had a bad one.
good death.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

born-digital artifacts.definition: Cultural and informational objects that are created, stored, and exist primarily in digital form rather than being digitized from physical originals.
born-digital artifacts.context: Born-digital artifacts are notoriously difficult to preserve in the long-term in the continuous battle against obsolescence and changing technology.
born-digital artifacts.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

infrastructural dependencies.definition: The underlying technical and conceptual systems—both hardware and software—that digital objects rely upon for their continued accessibility and functionality.
infrastructural dependencies.context: Digital objects are tied to infrastructural dependencies, both soft and hard, with multiple conceptual decisions that affect the manner in which they will (or should) be preserved.
infrastructural dependencies.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

duty of care.definition: The responsibility assumed by individuals or institutions to preserve and maintain digital materials and memories entrusted to them.
duty of care.context: The local storage of individual profiles became a duty of care for the digital memory of oneself.
duty of care.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

memory-keeping.definition: The active process of preserving, documenting, and maintaining records of past events, interactions, and collective experiences.
memory-keeping.context: With the end of Orkut and the deletion of their profiles, Orkut's users faced the responsibility of memory-keeping.
memory-keeping.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

orkontro.definition: In-real-life meetings and gatherings of groups that originally formed and connected through Orkut communities online.
orkontro.context: At the time, there was even a new category of gathering called orkontro which described IRL meetings of groups which had met on Orkut.
orkontro.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

community archive.definition: A preserved, read-only record of public online communities and their interactions, maintained after the closure of the platform that hosted them.
community archive.context: Orkut, the service, may be going away, but all of those incredible communities Orkut users have created will live on. We are preserving an archive of all public communities, which will be available online starting September 30, 2014.
community archive.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

platforms die by neglect.definition: The principle that digital systems, protocols, and services cease to function not only through active termination but through withdrawal of ongoing attention, maintenance, and support.
platforms die by neglect.context: As developer Sarah Friend argues in her essay Good Death, 'protocols live through attention, and they die by neglect.'
platforms die by neglect.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

collective memory.definition: Shared remembrances and cultural knowledge that groups of people construct together through common experiences and interactions.
collective memory.context: The preservation of the collective over the individual, the communion over the vanity, was a little triumph that ultimately did not last for long.
collective memory.source: The Death and the Death of Orkut

promise.definition: A central unifying grievance or shared vision that draws people into and orients a swarm toward collective action.
promise.context: These incidents coalesced into a single, potent grievance that acted as a 'promise,' drawing people into the swarm.
promise.source: The Swarm Effect: China's 2022 Covid Protests

broadcasting node.definition: A central hub or account that disseminates unified content to synchronize and orient a swarm's participants.
broadcasting node.context: In essence, Li served as a broadcasting node, helping to orient the swarm around its central promise.
broadcasting node.source: The Swarm Effect: China's 2022 Covid Protests

networked nature.definition: The characteristic of a swarm where participants are connected online through shared content and platforms before taking coordinated action.
networked nature.context: What set these protests apart from any that came before, including Tiananmen, is their highly networked nature. Before taking to the streets, protesters were already connected online, sharing and engaging with unified content.
networked nature.source: The Swarm Effect: China's 2022 Covid Protests

collective action potential.definition: The capacity of networked individuals to mobilize together for coordinated social action, which censors target for suppression.
